Existing resources such as the Quest for Orthologs benchmark service and OrthoBench provide valuable benchmarks grounded in real biological data and expert curation. However, the true evolutionary histories in all of these benchmarks are unknown, and therefore the true accuracy of orthology inference methods is unknown. Simulations provide an approach to evaluate accuracy where the complete ground truth is known. However, simulations are only useful for benchmarking if they realistically reflect empirical data. Here, we introduce OrthoSimulator, a Python package for generating realistic, empirically calibrated benchmark datasets with known orthogroups, orthologous relationships, gene trees, and evolutionary events. We demonstrate its utility by benchmarking widely used orthology inference methods across simulations calibrated from multiple methods and empirical datasets. We show that method-to-method variability in ortholog inference accuracy is robust to variation in simulation parameters. We further provide a detailed evaluation of ortholog inference accuracy through independent cross-validation, and show that OrthoFinder is the most accurate of the four methods tested. OrthoSimulator is freely available at https://github.com/lauriebelch/OrthoSimulator.

items.title: Survival-informed mutational network clustering reveals prognostic glioma architectures
items.corresponding_institution: INESC-ID, Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa
items.abstract: Cancer heterogeneity remains a major challenge for predicting patient outcomes. To address this challenge, we introduce SNOWS (Survival-iNfOrmed netWork cluStering), a probabilistic framework that integrates somatic mutations, clinical covariates and survival information to discover patient groups with distinct mutation patterns and survival profiles, using Bayesian networks to capture dependencies involving mutations and clinical variables. Applied to 950 adult-type diffuse gliomas from TCGA, SNOWS identified three clusters that transferred successfully to classify an independent CGGA cohort of 181 patients using mutation and clinical data, without requiring their survival outcomes. The transferred clusters showed distinct survival, mutation profiles and dependency structures, and provided prognostic information beyond WHO 2021 tumour subtype, age and sex, significantly increasing the C-index from 0.691 to 0.712. Cluster assignments were driven by specific mutation frequencies, with network dependencies improving the assignments of patients with less typical molecular profiles. Beyond glioma, SNOWS also improved prognostic discrimination in pan-kidney and pan-myeloid cohorts. These results support survival-informed network clustering as a general framework for resolving clinically relevant cancer heterogeneity.

items.title: Integrating Unsupervised Clustering with Transformer-Based Models for De Novo Cell Population Identification
items.corresponding_institution: College of Life Sciences, Nankai University, Tianjin
items.abstract: Single-cell transcriptome sequencing has been widely applied across the life sciences. It enables accurate and robust identification of cell types in heterogeneous biological tissues through unsupervised clustering, shallow learning, and deep learning. While deep learning does not outperform shallow learning in classification performance, it streamlines cell type identification by eliminating cumbersome preprocessing procedures. However, the availability of training datasets with comprehensive cell type annotations is always limited, so new datasets inevitably contain cell populations that are not pre-defined in the training data. To address this limitation, we integrated unsupervised clustering with transformer-based models to identify cell populations unrecognized by classical methods. Specifically, we developed the Nankai GeneRank Classifier by fine-tuning the pre-trained Geneformer-V1 model, and then clustered cells based on its softmax-normalized class probability matrix (SCPM). Applied to a public colorectal cancer dataset, the new method, named SCPM-based clustering, resolved cell populations that cannot be unambiguously identified by classical methods alone and led to the discovery of novel candidate markers of colorectal cancer stem cells, demonstrating its utility.

items.title: Scalable construction of near-wild-type brain atlases enables variability-aware neuronal identification in C. elegans
items.abstract: Matching cells across individuals is essential for comparing cellular data but becomes challenging when cell positions vary between animals. Here we introduce a framework for constructing probabilistic neuronal atlases by integrating partially overlapping observations from sparsely labeled, near-wild-type strains to reconstruct cellular organization from incomplete observations. Using five strains imaged without compression in a microfluidic array, we built an atlas of 129 head neurons (55 classes) that captures positional variability and infers spatial relationships even between neurons never observed together. We find that variability is spatially structured with neurons in compact regions being more stereotyped, while neuronal relative positions are more stable than their absolute positions. Exploiting these statistical relationships, variability-weighted identification improved top-1 accuracy to 86.3%, approaching human inter-annotator agreement, with the correct identity among the top three candidates in 98.2% of cases. Relationships stitched across strains reproduced observations in a held-out strain, and the atlas supplied correct identities in males and in pan-neuronal calcium imaging in vast majority of cases. Our extensible framework enables community-built atlases and offers a strategy for cell identification when anatomical variability limits template-based registration.

items.title: Restoring Marcenko-Pastur noise estimation and denoising of diffusion MRI under common image reconstruction
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Neuroradiology, University of Luebeck, Luebeck, Germany
items.abstract: Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging can reveal microstructure in the living brain, but the measurements are inherently noisy. Marcenko-Pastur denoising is a widely used remedy, helping to separate signal from noise under a simplified noise covariance model. However, we find that the model breaks under common image reconstructions across 28 public in vivo datasets, resulting in weaker denoising than intended. We restore the intended denoising behavior with a noise covariance model estimated from the reconstructed images, and validate the estimated model on repeated ex vivo and in vivo scans. The method requires no additional measurements or knowledge of the reconstruction, opening headroom for microstructure analyses in both existing and newly acquired data.

items.title: "The self" as shifting coalitions of brain systems in a continuous configuration space
items.abstract: Philosophers and psychologists distinguish many forms of self, yet neuroimaging results often implicate a shared core in the cortical midline or insula. We propose self-related processing arises from shifting coalitions of distributed brain systems, without a core. In a meta-analysis of 912 neuroimaging publications, titles and abstracts clustered into ten forms, including autobiographical memory, body ownership and interoception. No single location was significant in all ten associated brain maps, although each occupied different parts and amounts of midline and insular territory. Their differences were distributed across the brain. Regional patterns varied with study context, corresponded selectively with aspects of consciousness and resembled maps of general functions. Brain patterns combined at continuously varying strengths predicted regions reported in held-out publications better than single patterns or on/off combinations. Self-related processing therefore has no core and arises from shifting coalitions of distributed brain systems whose graded contributions define a continuous configuration space.

items.title: Generalized hippocampal replay exhibits memory recall-like dynamics
items.abstract: Hippocampal replay has been intensely studied for theorized roles in memory consolidation, credit assignment in reinforcement learning, and online planning. Much work in the field assumes that replayed trajectories traverse states smoothly and sequentially, in either forward or reverse order of experience. In a synthetic setting, we demonstrate that incorrect transition priors lead to systematic decoding error and show how model comparison addresses this issue. We compare a diverse set of transition models, including recall-like transition dynamics, and show how they can capture qualitatively different replay structures. Applying model comparison to three neural recording datasets from adult male rats, we find that the recall transition dynamics offer a statistically superior description of spiking during population burst events compared to a commonly used heuristic model of smooth trajectories. We propose a generalized conception of replay events through this theoretical connection to human free recall dynamics. Furthermore, our theory suggests that generalized replays may be a neural instantiation of online planning through generalized rollouts. We find preliminary evidence that generalized replays are more prevalent in settings where planning is beneficial. Overall, the proposed theory has implications for decoding methodology and the normative interpretation of hippocampal replay.

items.title: Electrostatic-hydrophobic cooperation in the mesoscale assembly of synapsin and synaptic vesicles
items.abstract: Synapsin associates with synaptic vesicles. How these local contacts give rise to a connected vesicle assembly remains unclear. We used a three-dimensional Brownian agent model to vary electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions independently at fixed particle abundance and confinement. With electrostatics alone, the agents representing synapsin approached almost every vesicle early, when most vesicles still belonged to separate groups. With both interactions active, a larger connected assembly formed earlier, more of these agents were near several vesicles, and they moved more slowly. Over the full 84 ms, the assemblies continued to grow under either interaction alone. By the final observation window, the two conditions had similar vesicle participation despite differences in protein association and contact composition. The positive early interaction contrast decreased as the assemblies grew. These observations distinguish local synapsin association from collective vesicle connectivity and identify a structural feature that can be measured alongside condensate formation.

items.title: Co-transcriptional splicing of the Drosophila Y-loop A transcript is organized in chromatin hubs and shows variable delay which increases with spermatocyte maturation
items.abstract: Splicing of the primary transcript is a major step to produce the mature mRNA. While the biochemistry of the splicing mechanism has been elucidated in detail, the dynamics and structural arrangements inside the nucleus are not clear. Biochemical and genomic studies of splicing and transcription most often lose the information about individual states and localization from the sub-nuclear to the tissue level by averaging over populations and homogenization of cells and tissues. Imaging approaches, which would overcome these problems, have been hampered by the short length of most genes, preventing discrimination between different regions like introns and exons along the transcript due to limited resolution. To overcome these limitations, we apply high-resolution microscopy with Airyscan joint-deconvolution to the megabase transcription units of Drosophila Y-loops. Along these extended chromatin fibers, we can directly observe the linear arrangement and local splicing events of introns and exons as well as the corresponding 3D chromatin structure. We compare these events between primary spermatocytes at different stages of their development within whole-mount testes. We show that co-transcriptional splicing of the Y-loop A transcript exhibits delayed splicing. The extent of this delay differs between transcription clusters along the same chromatin fiber within a nucleus and the average splicing delay increases with spermatocyte maturation. This shows that co-ordination of splicing and transcription is regulated locally at the site of transcription and by developmental state. We find that the concentration of the transcriptional activator Eaf is inversely correlated with spermatocyte maturation thus suggesting that the decreased frequency of transcription pause/pause release may be responsible for the splicing delay. Consistently, we find hubs containing the spliceosome with elongating and paused RNA-polymerase together with Eaf in chromatin bends. From their different arrangements we derive a model for splicing hub biogenesis.

items.title: Establishment and characterization of a brain cell line from bighead carp (Hypophthalmichthys nobilis)
items.corresponding_institution: Fuzhou Medical College (former Fuzhou Medical College of Nanchang University)
items.abstract: A wide range of pathogens continues to threaten bighead carp (Hypophthalmichthys nobilis) aquaculture. Fish cell lines allow host-pathogen interactions to be dissected and candidate control measures to be tested under defined conditions. We established and characterized the first brain-derived cell line from bighead carp, designated HnB, which is only the second cell line reported for this species. HnB cells exhibited stable proliferation in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) containing 5-20% fetal bovine serum (FBS) at 28-32 degrees C and were serially passaged more than 50 times. The species origin of HnB cells was confirmed by PCR amplification and sequencing of the cytochrome b gene, and the sequence obtained showed 100% identity with previously published H. nobilis cytochrome b sequences. The modal chromosome number was 48, and the cells were free of mycoplasma contamination. Transfection with pEGFP-N3 demonstrated that HnB cells support exogenous gene expression. Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) and viral titre assays showed that HnB cells were susceptible to spring viraemia of carp virus (SVCV). Moreover, both interferon alpha (IFN-alpha) and interferon-stimulated gene 15 (ISG15) were significantly up-regulated in HnB cells following exposure to SVCV or poly(I:C), whereas LPS down-regulated the expression of both genes, indicating that HnB cells mount transcriptional antiviral responses to viral and viral-mimetic stimuli. The HnB line therefore supports SVCV replication and gives a species-matched system for studying antiviral (IFN-alpha/ISG15) responses in bighead carp.

items.title: Smooth muscle KCa3.1 limits plaque progression and alters plaque composition in mice
items.abstract: Increased expression of KCa3.1 has been found in vascular smooth muscle cells (SMC), macrophages, and T cells in atherosclerotic lesions from humans and mice. While the efficacy of pharmacological inhibition and global silencing of KCa3.1 in limiting atherosclerosis has been demonstrated, the relative cell-specific contributions of KCa3.1 have not been determined. Therefore, we generated a smooth muscle (SMC) specific inducible KCa3.1-/- mouse with global Apoe-/- knockout (iSMKO) and assessed lesion development in the brachiocephalic artery (BCA) of tamoxifen vs. vehicle injected iSMKO mice on a Western diet (WD) for 15 or 40 weeks. In BCAs of iSMKO mice, lesion size and relative stenosis were increased and lumenal area decreased compared to vehicle injected mice. Additionally, iSMKO mice exhibited a significant reduction in SMC and collagen content at 15 weeks and 40 weeks, while macrophage content increased at 40 weeks. RNAseq analysis of BCA samples from tamoxifen and vehicle injected iSMKO mice prior to WD feeding (baseline) indicated increased mitochondrial function and PPAR-dependent signaling, similar to that found in prior studies of global KCa3.1 silencing. However, following 15 weeks of WD and induction of disease, these differences were no longer observed. Overall, this study provides the first cell-specific silencing of KCa3.1 to elucidate the contribution of KCa3.1 in smooth muscle to prior observations of KCa3.1 silencing. Our findings reveal both a beneficial role of SMC KCa3.1 in limiting plaque size and macrophage infiltration, and a potentially detrimental effect of reducing plaque SMC and collagen content. Combined with previous studies, this raises caution in the use of pharmacological KCa3.1 inhibitors in atherosclerosis and highlights the need for cell-specific targeting of KCa3.1 in optimizing potential therapies.

items.title: Centrosome identity drives asymmetric microtubule-dependent pushing forces, spindle positioning and daughter cell size
items.abstract: Mitotic spindle positioning is essential for tissue architecture and organogenesis. In Drosophila neural stem cells, spindle positioning is attributed to apically enriched Dynein generating pulling forces on astral microtubules (MTs). Surprisingly, however, we find that the mitotic spindle consistently adopts a basal position along the apico-basal polarity axis, challenging the canonical model. We show that centrosomes at opposite spindle poles retain an intrinsic asymmetry in MT nucleation capacity inherited from their mother-daughter identity, with the apical daughter centrosome nucleating more MTs than the basal mother centrosome. Equalizing or reversing this asymmetry alters spindle positioning, demonstrating that basal spindle positioning critically depends on asymmetric centrosomal MT nucleation. Centrosome photoablation reveals that astral MTs generate pushing forces against the cell cortex that drive basal spindle positioning, whereas reducing apical Dynein-dependent pulling exacerbates basal spindle displacement, revealing an unexpected role for cortical pulling in limiting spindle displacement. Consistently, 3D Cytosim simulations incorporating cortical pulling forces together with MT nucleation-driven pushing forces, either asymmetric (wild-type or inverted) or symmetric, reproduce the observed spindle positioning. Together, our findings reveal that centrosome identity establishes an intrinsic asymmetry in MT nucleation that converts astral MT pushing into a dominant directional force for spindle positioning. This mechanism counteracts cortical pulling and contributes to daughter cell size asymmetry, uncovering an unexpected role for centrosome identity in determining where cells divide.

items.title: Language-Driven Clustering of Transfer, Persistence, Prevalence & Recovery Studies for Forensic Activity-Level Evaluation
items.corresponding_institution: NZ Institute for Public Health & Forensic Science (PHF Science)
items.abstract: Transfer, Persistence, Prevalence, and Recovery (TPPR) data are essential for forensic activity level evaluations (ALE); however, concerns remain regarding the accessibility of relevant literature. This study investigated whether automated literature retrieval and natural language processing (NLP) methods could be used to identify and characterize TPPR studies. Existing forensic repositories were combined with records retrieved through the Web of Science Application Programming Interface (API) and enriched with bibliographic metadata, producing a corpus of 3,279 unique records. Automated retrieval tools were evaluated, and transformer-based topic modeling was applied to examine the breadth of the literature. The results showed that database APIs provided the most reliable mechanism for literature retrieval, while topic modeling identified meaningful groupings corresponding to major forensic disciplines and trace evidence types. The findings indicate that TPPR literature exists and that automated methods can support its discovery and organization. Although the availability of literature does not necessarily imply suitability for ALE, the results suggest that the principal challenge is the discovery, assessment, and reuse of published studies rather than their absence. Automated retrieval, semantic search, and quality assessment frameworks may improve access to relevant evidence and support the development of forensic knowledge systems for evaluative reporting and Bayesian network construction.

items.title: An apicomplexan-specific foundation model improves prediction of regulatory genomic signals in Plasmodium falciparum
items.abstract: Genomic foundation models learn transferable sequence representations through self-supervision, yet their practical value is contested. In data-rich mammalian genomes, task-specific models trained from scratch can match or exceed pretrained models on many regulatory prediction tasks. Whether self-supervised pretraining provides an advantage in small, data-sparse genomes has not been directly tested. We address this in the compact, 23Mbp, A/T-rich genome of the malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum. We trained a Genomic Pretrained Network (GPN) via masked-nucleotide reconstruction on 455 genome assemblies spanning 76 apicomplexan species. We then fine-tuned the model to predict a variety of epigenomic features in a held-out chromosome, including transcription factor binding sites, chromatin-accessibility, histone modifications, and 10 chromatin states. Pretraining followed by fine tuning improved prediction of most features, with most of the benefit concentrated on datasets with relatively little labeled data (fewer than 3,000 training examples). In contrast, a human-pretrained model transferred poorly, indicating that phylogenetically relevant pretraining, not foundation-model status alone, drives beneficial performance. Self-supervised pretraining on clade-specific assemblies is thus a practical route to data-efficient regulatory modeling in small genomes where training data is scarce.

items.title: Integrative analysis identifies LATS1 as a context-specific regulator of melanoma progression and immune response
items.corresponding_institution: Systems Biology Ireland, School of Medicine, University College Dublin, Belfield Dublin 4, Ireland
items.abstract: Malignant melanoma incidence is increasing, and survival remains poor following metastasis. The main driver oncogenes are BRAF and NRAS. Advancements in targeted agents and immunotherapies have improved survival rates, especially for patients with BRAF mutant melanoma. However, no targeted therapy options are available for patients with NRAS-mutant melanoma. Unfortunately, the development of resistance to all existing therapies remains a challenge. Recent evidence has shown that the MST2/Hippo pathway is deregulated in melanoma. The MST2 pathway core kinase LATS1 is a signalling hub that mediates the crosstalk between cell death and proliferation networks, and its inactivation has been related to melanoma progression and resistance to targeted therapy. However, the mechanisms by which LATS1 influences melanoma biology remain unclear. Here, to investigate this role of LATS1, we developed a lats1 knockout zebrafish melanoma model driven by either BRAF or NRAS mutations. Loss of Lats1 associates with reduced tumour-free survival in BRAF-mutant melanoma and a more invasive phenotype in NRAS-mutant melanoma, confirming a tumour-suppressive function. Integrating transcriptomics and proteomics datasets, we mapped molecular mechanisms mediated by Lats1 in tumours driven by these oncogenes, including pathways associated with the immune response regulated by Lats1. Subsequent validation in patient data confirmed an immune-evasive phenotype, associated with decreased LATS1 expression in BRAF-mutant melanoma. Additionally, the loss of LATS1 in NRAS mutant melanoma patients altered the expression of key DNA damage repair genes. Thus, this study identifies novel pathways controlled by LATS1 in melanoma, which aid in our understanding of the disease and offers new insights to be explored for the development of novel treatment strategies.

items.title: Dynamic multi-omics analysis of Adenovirus-induced rAAV-producing stable cell lines reveals the interplay between adenoviral infection and host cell metabolism
items.abstract: Recombinant adeno-associated viruses (rAAV) are invaluable delivery vehicles for gene therapy. However, to make rAAV-based therapies more accessible, there is a need to increase rAAV titers. Here we analyze the phenotypic variation among 30 Adenovirus-induced stably-transfected human producer cell clones to identify metabolic signatures associated with high vs low rAAV production. Exometabolomic characterization revealed decreased amino acid consumption in higher producers. Analysis of RNA-Seq data in the context of a genome-scale metabolic model identified upregulated carnosine biosynthesis-associated pathways during the first 6 hours post infection with adenovirus, relative to uninfected growth. Meanwhile, late infection timepoints exhibited increased amino acid release and de novo biosynthesis of serine, glycine, and arginine. Moreover, high producers decreased expression of genes linked with cholesterol biosynthesis and increased HMG-CoA degradation via HMGCL. Furthermore, sphingosine and ceramide biosynthesis genes were altered in high-producers in directions previously reported to resist cell death and suppress immune signaling. Overall, these findings elucidate the metabolic modulation upon adenoviral infection in a helper virus-induced AAV production process using stably transfected human cell lines.

items.title: Non-canonical subthalamic nucleus projections regulate motor variability
items.corresponding_institution: University of Maryland School of Medicine
items.abstract: Regulation of motor variability is a key hallmark of motor skill learning, balancing motor exploration with optimization of identified task solutions. Nevertheless, the underlying circuit mechanisms in the mammalian brain remain largely unknown. Subnuclei of the dorsal striatum in the basal ganglia promote stereotyped or variable behavior, respectively, and deep brain stimulation of the downstream subthalamic nucleus (STN) can alter motor variability. We therefore tested whether the STN regulates motor variability via non-canonical projections to striatum. We discovered that silencing STN neurons projecting to dorsolateral striatum impaired motor variability reduction in rats developing complex stereotyped movement patterns. In contrast, silencing STN neurons projecting to the anterior thalamic nuclei, or neurons in these nuclei that receive STN input and project to dorsomedial striatum, accelerated variability reduction. These results deepen our anatomical and functional understanding of subcortical motor circuits and reveal unknown roles for STN's non-canonical striatal projections in motor variability regulation.

items.title: Selective Gut-Related Biomarker Profiles Define Parkinson Disease Trait and State
items.abstract: Objective: Gut-brain-axis abnormalities are increasingly implicated in Parkinson disease (PD), but most studies examine individual biological compartments of this axis. We asked whether readily accessible stool and plasma-based biomarker profiles show broad or selective gut abnormalities in PD and whether the profiles associated with PD diagnosis (Trait) are the same as those associated with clinical severity (State). Methods: This cross-sectional study included 211 participants with PD and 204 healthy controls. Twenty-four stool and plasma biomarkers were organized into an overall profile, three parent domains (microbiome/dysbiosis, gut barrier/inflammation, systemic inflammation/immune activation), and eight more focused mechanistic profiles. Rank-based Global Statistical Tests (GSTs) compared PD Trait and State. Results: The overall profile showed no evidence of a PD vs. control difference (GST P=0.607; permutation P=0.521), whereas the domain of microbiome/dysbiosis differed (GST P=0.017; permutation P=0.013). Four of eight focused profiles differed nominally: microbial functional-groups, microbial functional-ratios, epithelial injury/bacterial translocation, and myeloid activation. Across PD clinical severity, overall-profile results differed (GST P=0.053; permutation P=0.037); both categories of microbiome/dysbiosis (GST P=0.023; permutation P=0.016) and microbial alpha-diversity (GST P=0.027; permutation P=0.031) differed. Interpretation: The analyses detected differences associated with PD Trait and State in selected gut-related profiles rather than a detectable overall PD-control difference. Microbiome-related profiles showed the most consistent domain findings across PD Trait and State, but they are sufficiently different to suggest that causation and progression of PD follow distinctly different gut processes. These findings refine the concept of the Parkinson gut and prioritize the microbiome for mechanistic and interventional studies.

items.title: Restrictive eating is linked to weaker recollection of food in young adults
items.abstract: Affective significance often enhances episodic memory, with stronger effects on recollection than on familiarity, but prior research has focused primarily on within-person manipulations of emotional valence. Here, we tested a novel question: whether stable individual differences in the personal significance of food were associated with long-term memory across individuals, given that food ranges from highly appetitive to strongly avoided. Across two experiments, we examined familiarity-based memory (using an image recognition task) and recollection-based memory (using a spatial source recognition task) for food and nonfood stimuli as a function of eating-related individual differences in young adults. In Experiment 1, familiarity-based recognition memory was largely unrelated to eating behavior. In Experiment 2, however, greater restrictive eating and fear of negative consequences from eating were associated with poorer recollection-based memory for food when compared to nonfood stimuli. Together, these findings suggest that individual differences in the affective significance of food do not correlate with episodic memory uniformly but instead are selectively associated with reduced recollection, but not familiarity, of food relative to neutral stimuli.

items.title: Human placental stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles ameliorate loss of intestinal stem cell subtypes in experimental necrotizing enterocolitis
items.corresponding_institution: Wake Forest University School of Medicine
items.abstract: Background: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a devastating intestinal disease in premature infants with epithelial barrier disruption and loss of intestinal stem cells (ISCs). While depletion of active ISC (aISC) populations has been reported in NEC, the impact of NEC on reserve ISC (rISC) populations during early postnatal development remains poorly understood. We examined developmental and disease-associated changes in ISC subpopulations and evaluated the effects of human placental stem cell-derived extracellular vesicle (hPSC-EV) therapy on ISC preservation and recovery. Methods: Experimental NEC was induced in neonatal rat pups through exposure to NEC stressors with animals assigned as breastfed controls (BF), NEC, or NEC treated with hPSC-EVs (NEC-EV). Ileal tissue was assessed histologically and immunostained for SOX9, OLFM4, HOPX, BMI1, and Ki67. ISC populations were quantified across early postnatal development (32, 56, and 96 hours of life), during NEC progression, and with EV therapy. Results: NEC caused significant histological injury accompanied by marked reductions in SOX9+ and OLFM4+ cells, indicating early and sustained loss of aISC populations. Among rISC markers in established NEC, BMI1+ cells were preserved, whereas HOPX+ cells were significantly reduced. Assessment of healthy early postnatal development revealed that SOX9+ and OLFM4+ cell numbers remained relatively stable, while HOPX+ and BMI1+ populations significantly expanded and were predominantly proliferative. Early NEC did not initially deplete HOPX+ cells but prevented their normal developmental expansion, resulting in the observed reduction of HOPX+ cell abundance during established disease. Treatment with hPSC-EVs significantly improved intestinal architecture and restored SOX9+, OLFM4+, and HOPX+ cell populations to near-control levels. Conclusions: NEC differentially affects ISC subpopulations in the developing intestine, causing loss of aISC and disrupting the expansion of HOPX+ rISC. Preservation and restoration of both aISC and HOPX+ rISC populations may contribute to epithelial regeneration and recovery. These findings identify HOPX-associated development and regeneration as potential therapeutic targets and demonstrate that hPSC-derived extracellular vesicles support ISC recovery and intestinal repair in experimental NEC.

items.title: Population-aware computational assessment of base-editing accessibility among pathogenic variants on human chromosome 21: an African-ancestry-focused pilot study
items.corresponding_institution: Thrivus University For Biomedical Science and Technology
items.abstract: Background Population-aware gene-editing research requires independent evaluation of clinical variant evidence, ancestry-stratified allele observations, nucleotide correction chemistry, and sequence-level editing constraints. We developed a source-traceable chromosome 21 pilot connecting these dimensions without equating computational accessibility with therapeutic editability. Methods Reviewed ClinVar pathogenic/likely pathogenic single-nucleotide variants were matched by GRCh38 chromosome, position, REF and ALT to overall and African/African-American (AFR) gnomAD v4.1 exome allele counts. Exploratory frequency contrasts used two-sided Fisher exact tests and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Higher-confidence variants with canonical adenine or cytosine base-editing chemistry underwent NGG PAM/editor-window screening, bystander enumeration, MANE v1.5 consequence annotation, theoretical joint-product assessment and chromosome 21-restricted guide-homology searches. Results Among 1,944 ClinVar variants, 851 matched gnomAD; 694 were quality-filtered and alternate-allele-observed overall, including 300 higher-confidence records. Six variants met exploratory AFR-elevation criteria. Of 234 higher-confidence ABE/CBE chemistry-compatible variants, 118 (50.4%) had at least one nominal NGG/PAM-window placement, 55 (23.5%) a nominal zero-bystander placement, and 44 (18.8%) a zero-bystander placement without an additional chromosome 21 NGG near-match within three mismatches. The 261 placements generated 295 hypothetical bystander events (195 distinct alleles); five distinct potential products overlapped pathogenic/likely pathogenic ClinVar alleles. Across placements, 764 theoretical target-corrected sequence states were enumerated, of which 503 contained at least one bystander. Three variant-level editing-accessibility comparisons between AFR-observed and AFR-unobserved alleles were not statistically significant (BH q=1.0). Conclusions Canonical correction chemistry substantially overestimates nominal local base-editor accessibility. A population-aware, transcript-informed computational framework can identify hypotheses for follow-up, but allele-frequency contrasts, guide-similarity results and enumerated sequence products do not establish clinical efficacy, experimental editing specificity or genome-wide off-target safety.

items.title: Sequencing of the Prnp-Prnd deletion junction in Prn-/- mouse tissues after formaldehyde fixation and >22 years at room temperature.
items.corresponding_institution: Institute for the Science of the Aging Brain (ISAB)
items.abstract: In 2004, Nicolas Genoud and colleagues reported that deletion of Prnd, which encodes Doppel, prevented neurodegeneration in mice with extensive Prnp deletions. The work tested the proposal that abnormal Doppel expression in the brain caused cerebellar degeneration in mice lacking the cellular prion protein, PrP. Advances in automated image analysis have expanded scrutiny of published figures, and post-publication reviews have raised concerns about apparent figure manipulation in this work, calling its authenticity and reliability into question. Here we assemble the surviving contemporaneous records of the original work and report new experiments on archived tissue. To reassess the reported genetic rearrangement, DNA from archived paraffin-embedded brain tissue was amplified across the putative deletion junction and analyzed by bidirectional Sanger sequencing and comparison with mouse reference sequences. The two reads spanned 607 positions and placed Prnp-side sequence, a 34-base loxP site and Prnd-side sequence in the expected order, with 93 intervening bases that matched bacteriophage P1 loxP-flanking and plasmid cloning-site sequences rather than the mouse reference and therefore probably derive from the targeting construct. Independent de novo reassembly from the 2025 Sanger chromatogram files reproduced the junction sequence; the assemblies differed only at three terminal bases with low base-call quality. These findings support the expected local junction arrangement and provide a publicly inspectable sequence description that extends the molecular information presented in the original paper. The amplicon size and the position of the loxP site match the values stated in the original paper, as does the approximately 18-kb distance between the two flanking sequences in the wild-type genome, which the deletion brings together. Recovery of junction DNA after more than two decades of room-temperature storage as paraformaldehyde-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue demonstrates the value of retained material for reassessing historical experimental claims.

items.title: AptaRender: an interactive drawing and styling tool for 2D nucleic acid structures
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biomedical Engineering, University of Texas at Austin
items.abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) diagrams are widely used to communicate nucleic acid secondary structure, yet the path from a sequence and pairing model to an editable publication figure often requires either specialized software or substantial cleanup in a general-purpose graphics editor. AptaRender (v2.3.1, available at https://yjhe99.github.io/aptarender/) is a browser-based editor that converts a set of user-supplied DNA or RNA sequences and their dot-bracket structures into an interactive 2D drawing. The software separates structure specification from visual composition: it does not predict folding, but provides direct control over the layout, nucleotide styling, base pair styling, numbering and export. AptaRender supports simultaneously working with multiple sequences, customized per-nucleotide sizing and coloring with customized styles, manual branching and motif repositioning, constrained rotation of helices around loop rings, and visualization of a user defined hybridization region between two strands. Drawings are exported as editable SVG or high-resolution PNG. The application is implemented as a single dependency-free HTML file that runs entirely in the browser and stores working state locally. This design makes the tool easy to distribute and suitable for rapid preparation of figures for manuscripts, presentations, and exploratory communication. AptaRender complements prediction and template-based visualization software by concentrating on lightweight, local, art directed figure construction. Across eight test cases, AptaRender reliably generated accurate, information-rich 2D nucleic acid structures and exported them in PNG and SVG formats, although specialized annotations and additional symbols required external editing.

items.title: Development of Novel NPC1-Targeting Autophagy Inhibitors for the Treatment of Uveal Melanoma
items.abstract: Background: Uveal melanoma (UM) is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults, and up to 50% of patients develop liver metastases. Metastatic UM responds poorly to conventional chemotherapy and currently available immunotherapies, highlighting the need for new therapeutic strategies. Because UM cells rely on lysosome-dependent stress-response pathways, including autophagy, we evaluated previously reported betulinic acid (BetA) derivatives and identified ALS-997 as a potent inhibitor of autophagic flux in UM cells. Methods: The anticancer activity of BetA derivatives was evaluated using the NCI-60 cancer cell line panel and WST-1 viability assays in UM cell lines and normal human melanocytes. Effects on autophagy and lysosomal function were assessed by western blotting for mTOR and autophagy associated proteins, LysoTracker Green imaging, and filipin III/LAMP2 staining. Apoptosis was evaluated by PARP cleavage and caspase-3 cleavage. The interaction of ALS-997 with Niemann-Pick disease type C1 (NPC1) was examined using a cellular thermal shift assay and computational molecular docking. NPC1 expression in UM cells and normal melanocytes was compared by quatitative PCR and western blotting. Results: ALS-997 preferentially reduced the viability of UM cell relative to normal melanocytes. Treatment with ALS-997 disrupted autophagic flux and lysosomal function, induced lysosomal cholesterol accumulation, and activated apoptotic signaling. ALS-997 also altered the thermal stability of NPC1, supporting cellular target engagement, while molecular docking predicted a direct interaction between ALS-997 and NPC1. NPC1 expression was higher in UM cells than in normal melanocytes. Conclusions: ALS-997 is a BetA-derived compound that disrupts lysosomal cholesterol homeostasis and autophagic flux, leading to apoptosis in UM cells. These findings support NPC1 as a potential therapeutic target in UM.

items.title: Benchmarking temporal causal discovery for fully and partially observed biochemical kinetic models
items.abstract: Accurately reconstructing networks of biochemical reactions is a crucial yet unsolved problem for leveraging advances in experimental techniques that track intracellular dynamics in a time-resolved fashion. This task is further challenged by the fact that we typically observe only part of the system, while many variables shaping the dynamics remain unobserved. Causal discovery methods can infer causal relations from purely observational data and account for unobserved variables. They therefore hold promise for yielding faithful, mechanistically interpretable representations of underlying biochemical interactions, but their potential in this context remains underexplored. In this work, we provide a systematic benchmark of state-of-the-art temporal causal discovery methods (tMIIC, PCMCI+/LPCMCI and SVAR-FCI) on time-series data from simulations of biochemical kinetics of mass action and Michaelis-Menten type modelled as systems of nonlinear stochastic differential equations, including an experimentally calibrated model of the epidermal growth factor receptor signalling network. By selectively omitting data, we consider the problem of reconstructing these networks in the presence of both latent confounders and unobserved species participating in reactions. We find that tMIIC and PCMCI+/LPCMCI achieve the highest overall prediction quality, with tMIIC able to handle larger samples within the same runtime budget. We identify, as the main condition for optimal performance of causal discovery, the consistency between data-sampling regimes (sampling intervals, trajectory length) and the typical timescales of the system. We establish that causal discovery can detect latent confounders via bidirected edges and unobserved species via time-delayed edges, locating hidden effects and encoding information on their typical timescales, provided that the data sampling guarantees adequate temporal resolution. As such, our results can guide the choice of hyperparameters in causal discovery algorithms and of data-sampling regimes to optimize network-reconstruction performance.

items.title: Preserved cognitive control with altered ventromedial prefrontal activity in lichen simplex chronicus: an fMRI study during the Multi-Source Interference Task.
items.corresponding_institution: Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile, Facultad de Ciencias Biológicas,  Santiago, Chile.
items.abstract: Lichen simplex chronicus (LSC) is a chronic pruritic skin condition, and one of its central features is the itch-scratch cycle. It has been hypothesized that resisting the urge to scratch, and thereby stopping this cycle, may depend on mechanisms of cognitive control. Here, we used the Multi-Source Interference Task (MSIT) during fMRI to examine whether patients with LSC (n = 9) differ from healthy controls (n = 11) in interference control or in the brain activity that supports it. Our results show that both groups had the expected interference effect, with no statistically significant group differences in behavioral performance or in cingulo-frontal-parietal BOLD activity. Whole-brain analysis revealed a greater interference-related decrease in ventromedial prefrontal cortex activity in patients than in controls. These exploratory findings show distinct patterns of brain activity in LSC while preserving interference control, warranting further investigation in larger samples.

items.title: Redox-driven control of 4-1BB interactome and signaling
items.corresponding_institution: Universite Cote d Azur, Inserm, CNRS, Institut de Biologie Valrose, Nice, France
items.abstract: 4-1BB (CD137/TNFRSF9) is a major immunoregulatory receptor, yet the molecular principles governing its intracellular signaling remain unclear. Here we show that the conserved cytoplasmic cysteine residues of 4-1BB are critical determinants of its interactome, enabling redox-responsive engagement of TRAF2 and LANCL2. Using quantitative assays combined with mutational analysis, we redefine the TRAF2-binding region and show that mild oxidation induces a cysteine-dependent disulfide stabilization of the complex. We identify that 4-1BB interacts with GPX1 independently of LANCL2, most likely indirectly via TRAF2, providing local antioxidant support when glutathione (GSH) is sufficient, whereas LANCL2, whose binding competes with GSH, is favored under mildly oxidative conditions. 4-1BB signaling was found to alter cellular redox balance, in which both TRAF2 and LANCL2 sites are critical. These findings reveal that 4-1BB functions as a redox-sensitive interaction hub, switching between distinct signaling states depending on intracellular redox conditions and the cysteine-dependent remodeling of its protein interactions.

items.title: sHSP-induced oligomerization enhances mammalian transcription factor potency
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Molecular, Cell and Developmental Biology, University of California at Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA, USA
items.abstract: Recently, a non-canonical role for small heat shock proteins (sHSPs) was identified, wherein sHSP-induced oligomerization drives targeted genomic accumulation of an endogenous silencing complex. Here we repurpose this property to develop sHSPs as compact, tunable tags for transcriptional engineering. Screening sHSPs across the tree of life, we show that sHSPs fused to transcription factors (TFs) can increase on-target genomic occupancy, recruit sHSP-tagged proteins, and amplify target-gene activation in mammalian cells. Distinct sHSPs vary in levels of transcriptional occupancy and output, providing a means to tune TFs activity while maintaining targeting specificity. This work establishes sHSPs as a new class of compact (~20kDa), tunable, activity-enhancing tags with broad potential for transcriptional engineering and synthetic biology.

items.title: Identification of JMJD1C as a key mediator of fibroblast remodelling in human AF by single-nucleus multi-omics
items.corresponding_institution: Experimental Cardiology, Department of Cardiovascular Sciences, KU Leuven, Leuven, Belgium; KU Leuven Institute for Single Cell Omics (LISCO), KU Leuven, 3000Le
items.abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most prevalent arrhythmia, accounting for up to 15% of arrhythmias in the elderly. Atrial enlargement associated with fibrotic and hypertrophic remodelling, termed atrial myopathy (AM), is considered a precursor to AF development. The mechanisms underlying the development of AM and its progression to AF remain incompletely resolved. To identify the unique and combined contributions of the major cellular mediators of AM and AF, we combine single-nucleus transcriptomics of human left and right atrial appendages (LAA and RAA) with paired RNA and chromatin-accessibility profiling of 20 LAA samples. We validate these findings through histological and functional studies in primary human cardiac fibroblasts (HCFs). Patients were stratified according to the presence of AF and AM (identified by left atrial volume dimensions; LAVI, Hi and Lo), generating Hi-AF, Hi-SR, Lo-AF and Lo-SR groups that separate AF-associated from structural-remodelling-associated alterations. Across 75,654 qualified nuclei, AF was associated with chamber-dependent shifts in cellular composition and gene expression, with extracellular matrix (ECM) and TGF-beta programmes prominent in LAA. Multiome analysis identified a stressed atrial cardiomyocyte (aCM4) state expressing natriuretic peptide A (NPPA) and natriuretic peptide B (NPPB), with altered cis-regulatory connectivity, and an inflammatory fibroblast (PTGDS+ FB) state characterised by IL-6 expression and matrix- and TGF-beta-associated programmes. Enhancer-driven network analysis identified GLIS3, TWIST2 and TBX20 as regulators of FB state transitions. The histone demethylase JMJD1C was enriched in PTGDS+ FB and induced by TGF-beta; its depletion attenuated alpha-smooth-muscle-actin (alpha-SMA) accumulation and reprogrammed TGF-beta-responsive transcription. Ligand-receptor analysis further predicted macrophage-to-FB TGF-beta signalling, showing the contribution of macrophages to the atrial inflammatory environment. These data define discrete aspects of rhythm- and structure-associated remodelling of human atrial tissue and identify a candidate macrophage-TGF-beta-JMJD1C-FB interaction for potential therapeutic development.

items.title: Single-cell and spatial multi-omics mapping of human ovarian aging across young and menopausal transition
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Gynecology, Women's Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine, Hangzhou, China
items.abstract: Ovarian aging is an early feature of human aging with broad consequences for women's health, yet its cellular dynamics across the menopausal transition remain unclear. We integrated single-cell transcriptomic, chromatin accessibility and spatial transcriptomic profiles across young, menopausal-transition and postmenopausal human ovaries. Granulosa cells (GCs) exhibited the most pronounced age-associated transcriptional remodelling. The menopausal transition was characterized by reduced DNA-repair activity and elevated stress-response programs in GCs, alongside broader changes in hormone-response and steroid-metabolic programs during ovarian aging. Integrated regulatory analyses implicated HEYL, a GC-enriched transcription factor, with reduced accessibility at a putative regulatory element during aging. Genetic analyses associated HEYL and its predicted upstream regulators with age at natural menopause, while spatial mapping revealed enrichment of menopause-associated genetic signals in GC-rich regions. HEYL depletion increased senescence-associated phenotypes in human granulosa-like cells and primary mouse GCs, whereas overexpression attenuated oxidative-stress-induced senescence. Perturbation of its orthologue Hey produced consistent effects in Drosophila ovaries. Together, our atlas reveals stage-associated granulosa-cell remodeling and implicates HEYL in ovarian aging.

items.title: A session-aware test protocol, energy-based strand pairing and a measured crossing-resolution limit for automated DNA knot identification in atomic force microscopy images
items.abstract: Atomic force microscopy (AFM) resolves the crossings of single knotted and linked DNA molecules, so the knot type can in principle be read from one image. TopoStats, to our knowledge the only automated pipeline for this task, assigns the correct type to fewer than 8% of the knots and catenanes in a public dataset of 721 molecules imaged in 20 sessions. Image classifiers appear to do better, but 18 of the 20 sessions contain a single knot type, so a classifier can score well by recognizing the session. We present three tools for evaluating and tracing these molecules. First, a session-aware protocol holds out whole imaging sessions, scores only the four classes not separable by size, and uses a probe to test whether images identify their session. Three classifiers reached 58-67% balanced accuracy on knots on their training sessions but only 27-32% under this protocol, near the 25% chance level, and the probe identified the session above chance in all eight tests. Second, an energy-based method connects strands through crossings by DNA length and stiffness. It traced the loops of 84% of knots and catenanes correctly, compared with 32% for TopoStats. Third, we measured the crossing-resolution limit of the pipeline. Labels derived from the known handedness of the knots gave the correct upper strand at 173 crossings without manual annotation, and the existing width rule ordered 137 of them (79%) correctly. A convolutional network did not exceed it. With the new pairing, the knot type was still correct for only 6-8% of knots and catenanes, because 72% of those with a valid pairing had lost crossings when closely spaced crossings were merged. Classifiers for AFM images should therefore be tested on new sessions, and further progress depends on resolving dense crossings. The protocol, labels and code are openly available.

items.title: Decomposing tissue-of-origin aging clocks reveals composite aging states across cancers
items.abstract: Aging is accompanied by tissue-specific molecular remodeling, yet whether tumors retain or depart from these programs remains unclear. In a pan-cancer analysis we show that age-associated molecular changes in tumors are organized by tissue of origin and partially mirror matched normal tissue trends. We introduce tissue-of-origin aging clocks to measure each tumor's deviation from its expected tissue aging, and ClockSHAP to decompose deviations into pathway-level contributions. Across breast and five other cancers, this decomposition reveals composite aging states in which youth-like deviations in proliferative pathways coexist with older-like deviations in damage-response and signaling pathways. In breast cancer, a clock trained only on normal tissues, applied without retraining, reproduces its deviations and pathway structure in two independent cohorts (~9,700 tumors), aligns with molecular subtype and TP53 mutation status, and predicts survival. These findings show how cancers reshape tissue-of-origin aging programs and provide a framework for applying and interpreting aging clocks in disease.

items.title: The role of shape and local features in human object recognition and learning
items.abstract: An object's shape is an important visual cue, critical for both perception and cognition. However, the current best models of human vision, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), do not prioritize shape, but instead, they rely on texture-like local visual features. This raises the question: Could shape be less important for human perception than previously believed? In seven experiments with both adults (N = 300) and 5-year-old children (N = 100), we tested the role of shape and local features in visual object recognition and learning. We found that humans could identify common objects as accurately using local visual features as they could using shape. This finding suggests that, like DNNs, local features may be sufficient for everyday visual recognition and that shape may not be necessary. However, we found that shape played a crucial role in novel object learning, allowing participants to even accomplish one-shot object categorization. Together, these findings force us to reconsider the role of shape in visual recognition and suggest that DNNs, despite not using shape, may nevertheless capture an important aspect of human visual processing.

items.title: Constrained Geometric Approach for Robust Local Optic Axis Estimation with Single Input Polarization Sensitive Optical Coherence Tomography
items.abstract: Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PSOCT) enables label-free, depth-resolved microstructure mapping in biological tissues, making it a powerful tool for studying myelinated fiber structures in the brain. Conventional single-input PSOCT measures cumulative retardance and apparent optic axis, which become inaccurate when fibers cross over depth. In single-input PSOCT systems, local optic axis estimation is challenging due to high noise levels, limiting the reliability of depth-resolved orientation estimation. In this work, we present a robust framework for local optic axis estimation in single-input PSOCT that incorporates physical constraints and polarization super-pixels. Polarization super-pixels serve as a preprocessing step to cluster spatially connected pixels with similar polarization states, increasing the effective signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and reducing instability in recursive matrix inversion. In addition, a physical constraint based on the mirror state of the input polarization is enforced during geometric fitting, significantly improving robustness and accuracy under noisy and low-SNR conditions. Experimental validation on ex vivo human brain tissue and phantoms demonstrates substantially improved stability and robustness of local optic axis estimation. This work enables reliable depth-resolved fiber orientation mapping in sophisticated fiber crossing scenarios and extends the potential of single-input PSOCT for analyzing structural connectivity at high depth resolution.

items.title: A Senescence-Like State is associated with the Immunosuppressive Phenotype of Tumor-Infiltrating Regulatory T Cells
items.abstract: Regulatory T (Treg) cells are essential mediators of immune suppression within the tumor microenvironment (TME) and represent a major barrier to effective anti-tumor immunity and to therapeutic efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Cellular senescence is traditionally characterized by stable cell-cycle arrest accompanied by distinct molecular and functional changes, yet whether tumor-infiltrating (TI) Treg cells acquire senescence-associated features and how these features influence their immunosuppressive activity remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that TI-Treg cells exhibit both apoptosis- and senescence-associated phenotype while retaining, and in some cases likely enhancing, their immunosuppressive capacity. Compared with peripheral Treg cells, some TI-Treg cells from solid cancers display elevated canonical senescence-associated markers, including p16 and p21, DNA damage response pathways, senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) and anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family genes, as well as activation of secretion associated beta-galactosidase (SA-beta-Gal). Though physiological Treg senescence leads to diminished immune suppression, TI-Treg cells paradoxically maintain the expression of key immunosuppressive molecules. These findings identify a previously unrecognized senescence-like state in TI-Treg cells that is functionally distinct from the loss of fitness typically associated with senescence in other cell types or aging-associated Treg senescence. Our study establishes senescence-associated reprogramming as a defining feature of TI-Treg cells and highlights the senescence-like state of Treg cells as a potential therapeutic target for selectively disrupting tumor immune suppression while preserving systemic immune homeostasis.

items.title: Development of lentiviral vectors specifically targeting CD4+ cells
items.abstract: Because of their central role in immunity, CD4+ T cells are a key target for genetic modification in many therapeutic applications, and lentiviral vectors with a VSV-G envelope are often used for this engineering. However, due to their broad tropism, these vectors are inadequate for cell-targeted in vivo gene delivery. Here, we explored using HIV-1 Env, which has a natural tropism towards these cells, as an alternative. We describe a three-plasmid vector production system to incorporate a panel of CCR5- or CXCR4-tropic Envs. These Env proteins are expressed from pCAG, a plasmid with reduced HIV-1 elements. We identify HIV-1 Env-incorporating vectors that can be produced with sufficient titres to specifically transduce primary CD4+ T cells in the context of in vitro mixed populations of peripheral blood mononuclear cells. We show efficient and specific transduction of HIV-1 Env vectors delivering an anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR). We demonstrate functional activity of the generated CD4+ CAR T cells, leading to the targeted killing of B cells in those mixed cell populations. Our methodology enables the production of HIV-1 Env-incorporating lentiviral vectors with defined CD4 targeted delivery, opening avenues for direct in vivo CAR T cell generation.

items.title: B-RANKO: An ncRNA Foundation Model with Bidirectional Decoder-Only Architecture
items.corresponding_institution: Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Computing, University of Zagreb, Zagreb, Croatia
items.abstract: Ribonucleic acid (RNA) plays central roles in gene expression, regulation and catalysis, and has emerged as an important target for therapeutic design. While recent RNA foundation models have achieved strong performance on representation learning tasks, relatively few approaches support both native sequence generation and transferable representation learning within a single framework. We present B-RANKO, a 150M-parameter bidirectional decoder-only ncRNA foundation model that introduces a novel bidirectional autoregressive attention mechanism, enabling a single architecture to support both de novo sequence generation and representation learning. Pretrained on a large corpus derived from RNAcentral, Rfam and GARNET, B-RANKO generates biologically plausible and thermodynamically realistic RNA sequences that exhibit strong novelty relative to their closest matches in the pretraining corpus. We further show that B-RANKO can be efficiently fine-tuned for aptamer generation and achieves competitive performance on BEACON, with particularly strong results on RNA engineering tasks. B-RANKO is publicly available on GitHub at filipvucenik/B-RANKO, together with usage examples and instructions for downloading model weights and datasets.

items.title: Rapid generation of marsupial induced pluripotent stem cells suitable for use in next-generation conservation
items.abstract: Marsupials account for a disproportionate share of recent and impending mammalian extinctions, that has prompted investment in the development of "next generation" conservation biotechnologies. These include the generation of genetically selected/modified individuals for improved population fitness. Given the inherent limitations of working with threatened species, a flexible vehicle to develop these technologies is through the generation and editing of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). However, it is deemed necessary to derive transgene-free iPSCs for conservation target species, which can be highly time consuming and expensive. This study describes the generation of iPSCs from the marsupial fat-tailed dunnart (diPSCs) that serves as a model species for next generation conservation initiatives. These diPSCs exhibit features of totipotency when cells are maintained with exogenous reprogramming factors for long periods, until differentiation potential is required. Neonatal dunnart fibroblasts were reprogrammed using doxycycline-inducible Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, Lin28 and Myc, and the resulting iPSC lines were characterised at the transcriptomic, epigenetic and functional level (trilineage differentiation, embryoid body formation and mouse blastocyst injection assays). Dunnart iPSCs exhibited robust transcriptional and epigenetic activation of core pluripotency factors (POU5F1, POU5F3, SALL4) as well as factors associated with the naive and primed states of eutherian pluripotency (TBX3, KLF2, TFCP2L1, SOX11, DNMT3A). Dunnart iPSCs readily differentiated in trilineage and embryoid body formation assays, where they expressed markers of all three germ lineages. When injected into 8-cell mouse blastocysts, dunnart iPSCs integrated into both the inner cell mass and trophoblast, reflecting a capacity to contribute to embryonic and extra embryonic lineages during early development. Further, we show that diPSCs can maintain their potential in the presence of exogenous pluripotency factors, until required for differentiation. This robust iPSC generation and maintenance approach is a valuable avenue for the rapid application of next-generation conservation technologies in threatened species.

items.title: Characterization and Evaluation of Hypoxia and LPS Preconditioned Placental Stem Cell Extracellular Vesicles in Immune and Intestinal Cells
items.corresponding_institution: Wake Forest University School of Medicine
items.abstract: Background: Human placental stem cells (hPSCs) have demonstrated therapeutic potential in experimental necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). Extracellular vesicles (EVs) secreted by the hPSCs contribute to these effects through paracrine signaling, however the molecular composition and biological activity of EVs can be influenced by culture conditions of the hPSCs. This study investigated whether hypoxic or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) preconditioning of the hPSCs alters the characteristics, protein composition, and biological activity of hPSC-derived EVs. Methods: hPSCs were cultured under normoxic conditions, exposed to hypoxia (5% O2), or preconditioned with LPS (50 {micro}g/mL). EVs were isolated from conditioned medium using ultrafiltration and size-exclusion chromatography, followed by characterized via nanoparticle tracking analysis, transmission electron microscopy, and single-particle detection of CD9, CD63, and CD81. Biological activity was evaluated in HIEC-6 intestinal epithelial cells through MTT, scratch wound closure, and nitrite detection assays. Immunomodulatory responses were examined in primary healthy neonatal rat CD4+ T-cell cultures using flow cytometry. Results: EV preparations showed comparable particle concentrations and size distributions across all three culture conditions, with no statistically significant differences. Vesicle-like morphology and EV-associated tetraspanins were detected in all preparations. All three EV groups improved epithelial metabolic activity following LPS exposure, enhanced scratch wound closure, and reduced nitrite accumulation compared with their respective controls. Flow cytometric analysis showed no statistically significant differences in TNF-, IL-17A, or FoxP3 expression among EV-treated CD4+ T-cell groups. Conclusions: Hypoxic and LPS preconditioning did not significantly affect the measured physical characteristics or secretion concentrations of the EVs. Although EVs from all three conditions showed beneficial effects on intestinal epithelial cells, neither preconditioning approach demonstrated a clear functional advantage over naive EVs in these simplified culture model. These findings suggest that preconditioning influences EV molecular cargo but more comprehensive biological function assays are required to delineate potential differences in effects on intestinal epithelial or T-cell functions. These data provide a basis for further studies examining its potential relevance to EV-based therapies for NEC.

items.title: The program STRUCTURE is good at detecting contemporary hybridization
items.abstract: The program STRUCTURE is widely used in conservation genetics to detect human-caused hybridization between previously isolated populations. However, its performance at this specific task is not yet known, and methods used to interpret the model output vary widely among studies. We simulated hybridization between two populations on the timescale of real-world cases and tested STRUCTURE's ability to correctly detect hybridization based on a simple "hybrid signal": inferring the presence or absence of a minimum of one hybrid. Overall, this returned the correct result in 100% of scenarios when Fst between the two populations was between 0.05-0.15 when using an optimal Q-threshold of 0.10. Performance was slightly reduced when divergence was very weak (Fst = 0.01, with an optimal Q-threshold between 0.30-0.35) or when the population receiving migrants was substructured, but it still returned the correct result in 89-100% of cases, depending on simulation parameters. We conclude that STRUCTURE, paired with this hybrid signal and our recommended Q-thresholds, is an appropriate tool for detecting contemporary hybridization.

items.title: TEV Induced Cleavage of Nuclei Tagged in Specific Cell Types (TIC-TaC) reveals histone profiles of activated neurons
items.abstract: Epigenomic profiling methods such as CUT&RUN/Tag are commonly employed to evaluate the genomic localization of histone modifications, transcription factors, and chromatin regulating proteins. Numerous transgenic mouse models also exist that label specific cell populations by leveraging Cre-based recombination and fluorescent reporters to allow for cell type specific epigenetic profiling in vivo. However, none of these systems allow for rapid, parallel processing for cell-type-specific CUT&RUN/Tag. Here, we report the development of TEV Induced Cleavage of Nuclei Tagged in Specific Cell Types (TIC-TaC) in which we leverage a recombination-based system that results in conditional expression of a Sun1-GFP fusion protein with a TEV site introduced between Sun1 and GFP. Like the existing INTACT system, nuclei tagged by cell-type specific Cre recombinase activity can be efficiently purified using immunoprecipitation to allow for rapid, efficient, and in parallel nuclei isolation. However, with the addition of TEV protease, TIC-TaC nuclei can be subsequently removed from the beads allowing for downstream CUT&RUN/Tag. We applied this system to neurons isolated from the cortex to define the effects of seizure induced neuronal activation on numerous histone modifications and histone variant proteins and identified concordant shifts in H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H2A.Z and H2BE at seizure responsive genes. Together, through the development and application of TIC-TaC to allow for parallel processing of tissue for cell-type specific analysis, we uncover activity-dependent regulation of chromatin in the brain.

items.title: PlantTV: a versatile user-friendly software to explore RNA-seq data across plant species
items.abstract: Bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) has become a central tool in plant biology for studying genome-wide transcriptional responses. However, interpretation of differential expression results remains challenging, particularly for non-model species where functional annotation resources are fragmented, heterogeneous, or incomplete. Existing user-friendly RNA-seq analysis platforms often rely on predefined annotation databases, limiting their applicability across the diversity of plant species. We developed Plant Transcriptomics Viewer (PlantTV), a free web-based platform for interactive exploration of plant RNA-seq datasets. PlantTV integrates differential expression analysis, expression visualization, functional enrichment analysis, and co-expression network exploration within a single graphical interface. A central feature is the Annotation Builder, which allows users to generate reusable annotation tables from diverse resources, including GFF/GTF files, EggNOG annotations, BLAST results, and custom tabular datasets. Using case studies in Arabidopsis thaliana, Malus domestica, and Eucalyptus melliodora, we demonstrate that PlantTV supports transcriptome analysis across a range of annotation scenarios, from well-annotated reference genomes to de novo transcriptome assemblies. PlantTV provides an interactive and species-independent environment for plant transcriptome analysis. By combining RNA-seq exploration tools with flexible support for custom annotation resources, PlantTV facilitates biological interpretation of transcriptomic datasets in both model and non-model plant species.

items.title: Spectrast: a multiscale spatial statistics toolkit for single-cell spatial transcriptomics
items.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics resolves gene expression in physical space, but the spatial statistics typically used to quantify spatial organization scale poorly to imaging-based datasets with hundreds-of-thousands of cells and thousands of genes. We recast the standard spatial-autocorrelation statistics as convolutions on a rasterized representation of the gene expression matrix and evaluate them with the fast Fourier transform. Measuring spatial statistics across multiple length scales becomes tractable for every gene using this approach, which extends naturally to differential reorganization testing between two tissue conditions.

items.title: Machine Learning-Enhanced Mucosal Luminal Interface Metaproteomics Reveals Diagnostic Potential of Microbial Proteins in Pediatric Inflammatory Bowel Disease
items.abstract: Abstract: Background: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), a chronic gastrointestinal disorder with two main subtypes, Crohn's Disease (CD) and Ulcerative Colitis (UC), is associated with more aggressive phenotypes and greater diagnostic complexity in pediatric patients. Conventional diagnostic biomarkers, lack sufficient distinguishing power between IBD subtypes. This study aimed to investigate and compare proteomic and metaproteomic profiles of pediatric IBD (PIBD) patients and healthy controls to develop a diagnostic panel capable of accurately diagnose IBD and distinguish its subtypes. Methods: We performed an in-depth evaluation of mucosal luminal interface samples from PIBD patients and healthy individuals, separately analyzing both the human proteome and microbial metaproteome data. The study involved selecting appropriate protein sets, employing feature selection techniques and machine learning across three intestinal regions: the terminal ileum, ascending colon, and descending colon. Results: Notably, panels composed solely of microbial biomarkers outperformed both human-only and combined human-microbial panels, achieving highly accurate results. Furthermore, the ascending colon emerged as the optimal sampling site, a result that aligns with the rich microbial diversity revealed in its taxonomic profile. Conclusions: Using a machine learning-based strategy on combined proteomics and metaproteomics, this study uncovered disease-relevant signaling pathways and delivered taxonomic as well as functional insights into the microbial dysbiosis of PIBD. A diagnostic panel built around microbial proteins (particularly those originating from the ascending colon) emerges as a promising tool for more precise stratification of PIBD subtypes. Larger, prospective studies are now needed to validate these candidate biomarkers and translate them into clinically deployable diagnostic panels. Keywords: Metaproteome, Biomarker, Pediatric Inflammatory bowel disease, Machine learning, Mucosal luminal interface.

items.title: Sisyphus at the splenic flexure: sidedness in colorectal cancer
items.corresponding_institution: Yale School of Public Health, Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, Yale Cancer Center
items.abstract: Colorectal cancer is divided into left and right to guide prognosis and therapy, yet a precise definition of left vs right sided colorectal cancer is still not fully agreed upon. The published conventions place it anywhere between the cecum and the rectosigmoid junction. The dichotomy assumes side homogeneity, i.e., that colorectal subsites within a side add limited information once the side is known. That assumption has been examined primarily through mutation prevalence, a quantity that confounds how often a driver arises with how strongly it is selected once it has. Analyzing 1,027 whole-exome and whole-genome sequenced colorectal tumors, we decomposed the prevalence of six driver groups into mutation supply and cancer effect, and asked whether a binary side label captures how each of their prevalence, mutation supply, and cancer effect vary along the colorectum. Mostly it does: the mutational input behaves as two blocks, and even the more than thirty-fold strengthening of cancer effect on BRAF V600E from sigmoid colon to cecum is adequately captured by side. But APC shows nominal evidence against side homogeneity in both prevalence and cancer effect while showing little net left-right difference, and PIK3CA H1047 rejects it in supply. The evidence for finer resolution is real but partial, and the failures do not announce themselves. We recommend additional research recording primary tumor location at the finest practicable resolution--at minimum, International Classification of Diseases for Oncology, 3rd Edition (ICD-O-3) topography. Such well-annotated datasets would enable the left-right boundary to be a reversible analytic choice rather than an irreversible annotation.

items.title: Multi-omic longitudinal profiling of companion dogs reveals cross-omic coordination and structured aging trajectories
items.abstract: Aging is a systems-level biological process shaped by coordinated changes across molecular, physiological, and environmental domains, yet how these domains interact and impact aging remains poorly understood. Companion dogs offer a powerful model for addressing this gap, combining shared human environments with diversity in genetics, lifespan, and disease susceptibility. Here, we present a longitudinal multi-omic analysis of aging in 965 companion dogs from the Dog Aging Project, integrating microbiome, epigenome, blood metabolome, and immune phenotyping with extensive clinical, environmental, and lifestyle surveys. We reveal an interconnected cross-omic architecture, with age emerging as the dominant axis of biological variation. We further identify a predictive multi-omic aging signature, distinguish linear from non-linear aging trajectories, uncover breed size-dependent dynamics, and characterize omic-specific mortality risk. Collectively, our findings reveal organizing principles of aging, many paralleling human observations, provide a unique resource for integrative geroscience, and establish dogs as a translational model for aging research.

items.title: The ANKLE2-VRK1 pathway promotes neuronal resilience by preserving proteostasis during aging
items.abstract: ANKLE2 is a key regulator of neural stem cell division through inhibition of the kinase VRK1, and mutations in either ANKLE2 or VRK1 cause rare neurodevelopmental disorders that impact brain growth and development. Recent evidence showing that reduced ANKLE2 activity promotes Tau aggregation in vitro suggests that ANKLE2 may also contribute to age-related neurodegenerative processes; however, its role post-development remains unknown.
