C3PO recovers structure associated with known latent variables across a variety of data sets without access to those variables during training. It identifies dynamics on timescales from tens of milliseconds to hours and reveals previously unreported representations and their dynamics. These results establish C3PO as a powerful tool for uncovering interpretable structure in high-dimensional point-process data sets.

items.title: α-Synuclein structural heterogeneity associates with distinct cytopathologies in multiple system atrophy
items.abstract: Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is characterized by oligodendroglial -synuclein inclusions, although neuronal inclusions also occur. We investigated whether regional differences in -synuclein filament structure are associated with distinct cytopathologies in a neuropathologically confirmed MSA brain by comparing the medial temporal lobe, which showed prominent neuronal inclusions and limited oligodendroglial pathology, with cerebellar white matter, which contained exclusively oligodendroglial inclusions. Cryo-electron microscopy resolved filaments from these regions at 3.0 [A] and 2.0 [A], respectively. Medial temporal filaments contained a previously undescribed protofilament fold, PF-IIIA, paired with canonical PF-IIB2, whereas cerebellar filaments adopted the canonical MSA Type II structure. PF-IIIA exhibits extensive remodeling of its core while retaining the asymmetric doublet architecture. These findings reveal regional -synuclein structural heterogeneity within a single MSA brain and suggest a potential association between distinct filament conformations and neuronal versus oligodendroglial cytopathology, highlighting the importance of regional and cellular context in filament organization and disease heterogeneity.

items.title: A digital twin of freely moving mouse V1 learns a general visual code bridging classical physiology and active vision
items.abstract: Decades of controlled experiments in passive, head-fixed animals have characterized the response properties of mouse primary visual cortex (V1) and their strong modulation by behavioral state. However, in natural vision the animal is active, continuously shaping its own visual input as it moves and coupling vision to behavior. To bridge this gap between classical controlled experiments and natural vision, we trained a multimodal digital twin to predict V1 spiking in freely moving mice from retinocentric video together with locomotion, pupil, and eye and head movements, then froze it and probed it in silico under controlled conditions. The representation it learned generalized across stimulus classes, animals, and recording regimes. Although never trained on parametric stimuli or given cell-type labels, the model recovered V1's canonical tuning for orientation, spatial frequency and contrast, including the systematic differences between putative excitatory and inhibitory cells. A single model transferred to new mice from a few minutes of recording. Without retraining, it matched the representational geometry of an independent head-fixed dataset of natural movies as closely as two recorded mice match each other. Behavior modulated most V1 neurons, and clamping each variable in turn showed that locomotion and pupil dilation share a gain increase, while only locomotion shifts sensitivity toward high spatial frequencies. By learning this representation from the freely behaving animal and probing it under controlled conditions, freely moving digital twins bridge classical visual physiology and active vision.

items.title: Structure learning and context inference emerge from next-state prediction in a cerebellar-medial temporal lobe circuit
items.abstract: Humans learn many context-dependent behaviors; yet the contexts driving these behavior are rarely explicit and must instead be inferred. Further, we are rarely exposed to the same context multiple times, so we must learn how to generalize to new contexts from our experiences in prior ones. Motor learning relies on both. People can hold multiple conflicting visuomotor mappings and recall the appropriate mapping when needed. Much as cricket is easier to learn for someone who already plays baseball, experience with previous mappings accelerates learning of others. Indeed, human motor learning is well described by context inference, in which the learner infers the context and uses it to update and recall the appropriate memory. How the brain implements this inference, and which circuits perform it, however, is unknown. Here we introduce a circuit in which a cerebellar forward model predicts the next state conditioned on a latent from the medial temporal lobe. At the same time, the medial temporal lobe updates that latent from the cerebellum's prediction error. While we only trained the circuit to predict next state, it learns to infer context and represents contexts in a structured latent space. Coupled with this latent, a motor cortex module reproduces context-dependent retrieval, savings after washout, spontaneous recovery, and evoked recovery, and compensates for perturbations it has never experienced. The same circuit reproduces cerebellar-dependence of object-location memory and independence in object-recognition memory, loss of place-cell stability in the dark when cerebellar plasticity is blocked, and the abstract geometry of hippocampal activity in a reversal task. Cerebellar-medial temporal lobe interaction is therefore a candidate locus for context inference and structure learning in the brain.

items.title: Preparatory Bias Currents Alone Write Letters and Words in a Fixed Recurrent Circuit
items.abstract: We show that preparatory input currents, or bias currents, alone can make a recurrent circuit with fixed weights write all 52 cursive letters, and words built from them. Each letter is produced by its own bias pattern, ramped in as a preparatory drive and withdrawn at a go cue; the recurrent weights and the readout never change, and the readout's weights are random, with a single global gain picked on four letters (a-d). We take the stability-optimized circuits (SOCs) of Hennequin et al. and extend them with mutual inhibition: all inhibitory neurons inhibit one another through a single shared weight (MISOC, mutual inhibition SOC). With 200 units, the pen of the SOC stays on average 1.7% of a letter width from the target over all 52 letters, and that of the MISOC 0.9% (25 random circuits; R2 = 0.996 and 0.999). The other 48 letters are learned through their bias patterns alone, without changing a single synapse, so new letters cannot disturb old ones. Letters learned one at a time chain into words in one continuous run. Mutual inhibition improves the circuit: with a shared weight of 0.5 the MISOC writes with 16-48% less error than the SOC at every network size tested (50 to 200 units), and with fifty network-derived input channels instead of one bias per neuron it keeps its advantage. Bias currents and mutual inhibition let small, fixed circuits hold a large and growing motor repertoire and switch within it without any synaptic change.

items.title: Longitudinal examination of cerebellar morphometry across typical aging adults reveals nonlinear heterogenous trends
items.abstract: Cerebellar structural integrity has been associated with cognitive capability in both neurodegenerative and healthy aging populations. The understanding of regional, longitudinal cerebellar structural changes is not well studied, and with an increasing aging population, there is an increasing need to fill this gap. Moreover, traditional modeling approaches apply linear techniques, which may fail to detect possible nuanced aging patterns. The present study investigates the nonlinear effect of age on subregional cerebellar structures in healthy adults (n = 1,371), aged 36 to 90+, from the Human Connectome Project in Aging and the follow-up continuation, Aging Adult Brain Connectome studies. Subject T1w images underwent cerebellar segmentation and volumetric estimation via the Automatic Cerebellum Parcellation using U-NET with Locally Constrained Optimization (ACAPULCO) algorithm. Cross-sectional, longitudinal, and sex specific volumetric differences were examined using generalized additive mixed models. Heterogenous atrophy patterns were observed across the cerebellum; however, the majority of effects were evident in the posterior cerebellum. Longitudinal models showed nonlinear negative trends for all regions surviving correction, while baseline age effects had a combination of linear and nonlinear negative trajectories after correction. Specific sex differences emerged, where men predominantly had higher regional volumes, as well as there being sex-related influences of longitudinal morphologic patterns. Furthermore, midlife appeared as a period of structural vulnerability, demonstrating escalated volume loss. Consistent with the literature, the identified volumetric reduction patterns suggest that age effects on the cerebellum are multifaceted, with region specific alterations, highlighting the complexity of this structure.

items.title: Circuit decoupling with surrogate compensation for baseline tuning in biophysically detailed neural models
items.corresponding_institution: Center for Biomedical Imaging and Neuromodulation, Nathan Kline Institute for Psychiatric Research, Orangeburg, NY, USA
items.abstract: The baseline regime of a neural circuit shapes its dynamical behavior. Establishing an appropriate baseline is therefore an important part of tuning a computational circuit model. This baseline can be specified in terms of target population firing rates and achieved by adjusting the background inputs to each population. Due to recurrent coupling, these inputs need to be tuned jointly, requiring a high-dimensional search that is especially costly for biophysically detailed circuit models. This remains a major bottleneck since current optimization methods are limited in their ability to tackle this problem. Decoupling the circuit by removing all the connections between its cells allows background inputs to be tuned independently, but the solution may not hold when the connectivity is restored. We developed a compensated decoupling method in which missing recurrent inputs are replaced by surrogate inputs from spike generators firing at the corresponding target rates. The resulting input approximates the recurrent drive expected at the target regime, so the background inputs tuned in this setup may remain valid after restoring connectivity. We applied the method to a 43-population biophysically detailed model of the macaque auditory thalamocortical circuit, which had previously proved challenging to fit closely to experimental data. First, we tuned the background input independently for each population in the fully decoupled setup. Next, we tested the solution in the isolated cortical and thalamic subcircuits, preserving recurrent connections within each subcircuit. The cortical subcircuit had two coexisting regimes and settled into the off-target one by default. A gradual transition from surrogate to recurrent self-excitation allowed it to reach the near-target regime. The thalamic subcircuit exhibited a single regime deviating from the target due to imperfect surrogate compensation. Jointly tuning a separate tonic input correction for each thalamic population substantially reduced the errors. Finally, we tested the solution in the full thalamocortical circuit, combining the tuned background inputs, thalamic corrections, and gradual restoration of self-excitation. The full circuit consistently reached a near-target regime across multiple random model realizations. The approach yielded an improved macaque auditory thalamocortical baseline model, providing a community resource for investigating the auditory thalamocortical system's dynamics. Together, the results demonstrate that our method can facilitate baseline tuning in a biophysically detailed model by enabling decoupled optimization and guiding subsequent refinement.

items.title: NeuroMASS v4: Geometry-Aware Neural Population Dynamics via Learnable Hyperbolic Latent Representations and Biologically-Calibrated Diagonal State Space Models
items.abstract: The geometry of neural population activity is a fundamental challenge in computational neuroscience. We present NeuroMASS v4, a novel architecture that introduces learnable hyperbolic latent geometry to spike-train co-smoothing on the Neural Latents Benchmark (NLB'21). Our central scientific claim is that the curvature c of a Poincaré-ball--learned end-to-end from extracellular spike recordings--constitutes a biologically interpretable geometric signature: significantly positive for ring-manifold motor circuits (MC_Maze, MC_RTT) and near-zero for topologically unstructured frontal circuits (DMFC_RSG). The architecture unifies five principled components: (i) discrete spike-count embed- dings with learned neuron-identity vectors, (ii) permutation-equivariant attention-weighted neuron pooling, (iii) a diagonal S4D state space model initialised with a log-uniform frequency prior spanning 2-200 Hz, (iv) a Poincaré-ball projection with learnable scalar curvature, and (v) a Frobenius-bounded session adapter. Training uses masked self-prediction of spike counts with an auxiliary behaviour decoding objective; all experiments use exclusively real DANDI/NLB recordings under a strict fail-stop data policy. We report results across four NLB datasets spanning motor, somatosensory, and cognitive cortices in rhesus macaque, and demonstrate that learned curvature statistically predicts circuit topology.

items.title: LSm4 methylation contributes to hydrogen sulfide-mediated stomatal closure
items.corresponding_institution: Instituto de Fisiologia Biologia Molecular y Neurociencias
items.abstract: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) expand proteomic diversity, yet how redox PTMs intersect with post-transcriptional regulation remains poorly understood. Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) signals partly through cysteine persulfidation. Here, we investigated the relationship among persulfidation, protein arginine methyltransferase 5 (PRMT5)-mediated methylation, and alternative splicing in Arabidopsis. Proteomic data revealed an enrichment of splicing factors among persulfidated proteins and PRMT5 targets. We focused on LSm4, a U6 snRNP component, and GRP7, a splicing modulator. We show that both proteins are persulfidated in vivo, independently of PRMT5-targeted arginine residues, whereas H2S availability positively influenced their PRMT5-dependent methylation. These findings reveal a connection between H2S signaling and PRMT5-dependent methylation, prompting us to explore their convergence in alternative splicing regulation. Transcriptome-wide analyses revealed substantial overlap between genes exhibiting H2S-responsive alternative splicing and those with LSm4 methylation-dependent splicing changes. These transcripts were enriched in functions related to RNA processing, immune responses, and stomatal movement. The prmt5 mutant and plants expressing methylation-deficient LSm4 were impaired in H2S-induced stomatal closure. Furthermore, H2S-responsive splicing was more pronounced in guard-cell-enriched epidermal samples than in mesophyll-enriched samples. Together, our findings identify PRMT5-dependent LSm4 methylation as a link between H2S signaling and alternative splicing, with functional implications for stomatal regulation.

items.title: Functional specialization of LC3B and LC3C in autophagosome biogenesis and cargo degradation: Relevance of the N-terminal region.
items.abstract: ATG8 proteins are key regulators of autophagosome biogenesis and maturation. Despite extensive research on human ATG8 family members, the functional differences between individual proteins remain poorly understood. Among them, LC3C is one of the least characterized members. However, its involvement in a growing number of cellular processes has attracted increasing interest in understanding its specific functions. Here, we investigated the functional specialization of LC3C using HeLa ATG8 Hexa-knockout cells individually reconstituted with GFP-LC3C or GFP-LC3B. This experimental system allowed us to examine the specific properties of each protein independently of other ATG8 family members. Under starvation conditions, LC3C formed more numerous and larger autophagic vesicles than LC3B, while both proteins sustained autophagic flux. Furthermore, proteinase K protection assays confirmed that both proteins could promote autophagosome closure. The two proteins also differed in their ability to promote the autophagic degradation of specific cargo receptors, with LC3B being more efficient in p62 degradation and LC3C in NDP52 degradation. Confocal microscopy revealed that LC3B and LC3C predominantly localized to distinct autophagic vesicles, suggesting their association with different autophagosome subpopulations. Finally, analysis of chimeras generated by exchanging regions between LC3B and LC3C revealed that the N-terminal region of LC3C determines autophagic vesicle size, whereas its ubiquitin-like core influences intracellular localization. Together, these results suggest that LC3C contributes to determining specific autophagosome properties, such as their size and intracellular localization, expanding our understanding of how individual ATG8 proteins regulate the autophagic process.

items.title: Sequential co-translational assembly of the yeast SAGA DUB module precedes post-translational core docking.
items.abstract: The 1.8-megadalton SAGA coactivator is organized into discrete functional modules, yet how individual catalytic modules are assembled and integrated into the holo-complex remains poorly understood. Here, we dissect the assembly pathway of the four-subunit histone H2B deubiquitinating (DUB) module in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Pairwise RIP-qPCR uncovers a unidirectional network of co-translational interactions sequentially linking Sus1, Sgf11, Ubp8, and Sgf73. Combining systematic deletion genetics with co-immunoprecipitation and quantitative NanoBiT assays in intact living cells, we demonstrate that these contacts form an obligate linear cascade rather than independent binary events: each upstream subcomplex licenses the next nascent-chain engagement, sustains downstream Sgf11 and Ubp8 stability, and precludes post-translational bypass. Conversely, DUB subunits exhibit no co-translational interactions with the SAGA core interface, indicating that completed modules dock post-translationally. Thus, unlike single-scaffold assembly models, SAGA separates multi-step co-translational module templating from post-translational holo-complex docking, safeguarding compositional fidelity.

items.title: Learning gene co-regulation across cells with Multicellular Transformer
items.abstract: Understanding how genes coordinate across cells is central to explaining tissue function and disease, yet most existing models still take a single cell as input and therefore emphasize cell-intrinsic regulation. We present the Multicellular Transformer (MCT), a foundation model built around a different assumption: cells function together within tissues, so the appropriate unit of input is not one cell in isolation but a set of cells from the same sample. By jointly modeling multiple cells, MCT learns context-aware gene embeddings that capture gene-gene interactions across the tissue environment. Trained on a large set of tissue samples (>4200) across more than 30 tissue types, MCT recovers ligand-receptor interactions, infers cross-cell signaling programs, and reveals spatial co-localization patterns directly from scRNA-seq data. Its contextual embeddings identify disease-specific rewiring of gene neighborhoods in systemic lupus erythematosus and COVID-19 and predict population-level perturbation effects in cancer without additional training. By linking gene-level regulation to tissue-scale organization, MCT provides a scalable framework for modeling multicellular biology and enables in silico discovery of therapeutic targets and tissue-specific dependencies.

items.title: Paired multiomic profiling defines the healthy human synovium infrapatellar fat pad stromal continuum
items.corresponding_institution: The Scripps Research Institute, La Jolla, CA
items.abstract: The synovium and infrapatellar fat pad (IPFP) are anatomically contiguous tissues implicated in osteoarthritis, yet their cellular and molecular organization in the healthy human knee remains poorly defined. We combined bulk RNA sequencing with paired single-nucleus transcriptomic and chromatin accessibility profiling to establish a quantitative multiomic reference of healthy human synovium and IPFP. Analysis of 54,716 nuclei from six cadaveric donors identified 23 synovial and 20 IPFP cell populations and indicated that the two tissues share one transcriptionally continuous, largely quiescent stromal compartment. Stromal populations shared core transcriptional programs but differed primarily in extracellular matrix output, with transcripts of inhibitory regulators predominating over those of their functional opponents. TIMP3 exceeded MMP14 in 42 of 43 single-nucleus populations across both tissues and by 13- to 39-fold in bulk tissue. Chromatin accessibility primarily distinguished stromal lineages and resolved transcriptionally defined subtypes, separating synovial lining from sublining fibroblasts and adipocytes from fibroblasts. Fibroblast and adipocyte populations occupied a common transcriptional trajectory accompanied by declining expression of organelle-turnover programs and little proliferation, with no dividing adipocytes and fewer than 0.05% of fibroblasts in the cell cycle. Despite this shared organization, the IPFP exhibited greater inferred intercellular signaling, attributable in part to BMP5, which was not detected in synovium. These findings describe healthy synovium and IPFP as regionally specialized parts of a transcriptionally continuous stromal compartment and provide a quantitative reference for identifying cellular and regulatory changes in joint disease.

items.title: Expanded ME-model analysis capabilities enable genetic recoding, proteostasis, RNA decay, and cofactor essentiality in bacterial models
items.abstract: Genome-scale metabolic models (M-models) are widely used to understand and manipulate microbial metabolism in silico, and are characterized by an extensive availability of automated reconstruction, analysis tools, and simulation software. The scope and accuracy of M-models was greatly improved by the development of metabolic and gene expression models (ME-models) aimed to infer the optimal allocation of individual macromolecules such as proteins, RNA, and enzymatic complexes which constrain metabolic fluxes to their availability and abundance. Although ME-models reconstruction and simulation is currently aided by open-source software such as coralME, COBRAme, ECOLIme, and solveME, they lag behind their M-model counterparts and lack formal analysis tools such as gene essentiality analysis, that would facilitate a broader adoption of ME-models in research. Moreover, the rigid and incomplete formulation of ME-models limit advanced analyses they are theoretically capable of, including the simulation of genomically recoded organisms, protein homeostasis, enzyme cofactor essentiality, and RNA decay. Here, we present coralME v1.3, a vastly improved software version aimed to expand the applicability of ME-models by adding support for translation of non-canonical amino acids, protein and RNA degradation reactions, use of arbitrary coupling coefficients and parameter values, and formalized gene and cofactor essentiality analyses. This work expands, formalizes, and streamlines ME-model reconstruction and analyses for applied research.

items.title: Genomic tessellations
items.abstract: Periodicity is ubiquitous in genomic data. Assembled sequences are dense with homopolymers, microsatellites, and large satellite arrays, which contribute to phenotype, variation, and disease. Third-generation sequencing technologies, such as Oxford Nanopore (ONT) and PacBio HiFi, has enabled longer and increasingly accurate reads, but have brought with them systematic error biases in repetitive regions, where insertions and deletions can distort array lengths and mimic or obscure biological variation. This periodicity is not benign: local repetitiveness makes sequence alignment ambiguous and genome assembly error-prone. In sequence analysis, these two manifestations of periodicity are simultaneously at play, each compounding the challenges of the other; a unified representation of repetitive and non-repetitive sequence is necessary to account for their combined effects consistently. We propose a paradigm under which (either repetitive and non-repetitive) DNA is split into its identity (its irreducible components) and its geometry (how its components are realized). A genomic tessellation {tau} is a canonical factorization of any sequence S of length n over the DNA alphabet into a sequence of tiles partitioning S, where each t in {tau}S is described as a quasi-periodic run of a canonical unit identity ut with geometry consisting of span st, phase {varphi}t, and a set of exceptions Xt. We show that, for a prescribed error bound k [≥] 1 and fixed maximum unit length P, S can be tessellated in O(n) time such that every tile has a unique identity whose periodic expansion differs from the tiled sequence by at most k edits, and that tiles sharing an identity are related by a bounded number of geometric adjustments. We introduce the tessellated Burrows-Wheeler transform (tBWT), which indexes {tau}S by concatenating, over all tiles in order, the identity ut of each tile. For a tessellated query q of m tiles, the tBWT counts the repeat-agnostic occurrences of q in O(m) time, and for sampling interval r locates its h occurrences in {tau}S in O(m + hr) time. We demonstrate that tessellations avoid the well-known speed-accuracy tradeoff and outperform state-of-the-art long-read mappers in repeat-dense regions in both speed and accuracy. On a 20x simulated set of both ONT and HiFi reads on the HG002 maternal X chromosome with synthetically-expanded repeat arrays, locating and chaining exact tile identity matches obtained from the tBWT is up to 57x and 83x faster, respectively, than the state-of-the-art mappers minimap2 and Winnowmap2, with comparable accuracy. Furthermore, by abstracting away differences in geometry, tessellations of a set of input sequences onto itself (an autotessellation) reveals homology otherwise obscured by array-length variation and local sequence divergence. A geometry-only polishing of an an ONT-only assembly of the HG002 maternal X chromosome with [~]50x PacBio HiFi reads improves assembly QV from 45.4 to 60.6 in under a minute using less than 10GB of memory. Tessellated-read evidence over the autotessellation of this assembly organizes 167 mitochondrial contigs totaling [~]4 Mbp into a single family with a [~]16.5kbp representative, which aligns to the HG002 Q100 mitochondrial genome with 100% identity. Genomic tessellations provide a canonical representation of repetitive and non-repetitive DNA and enable efficient sequence analyses while preserving homology.

items.title: Visual Illusion: A Matter Of Disorder Between Retinal And Perceived images
items.abstract: Visual illusions reveal that perception is constructive rather than a faithful copy of the retinal image. This paper proposes that the brain supplements ambiguous or incomplete sensory input with virtual edges, filled-in surfaces, brightness and size cues, and illusory contours. Using gray-level Shannon entropy, we compared original and perceived images across five illusion classes: edge detection, surface filling-in, brightness perception, size perception, and the Hermann grid. In all cases, perceived-image entropy exceeded real-image entropy. These findings support a unified account of visual illusions as constructive inference: the brain introduces additional information to achieve global coherence, reflecting a trade-off between low-entropy processing and perceptual interpretation.

items.title: Tracking single neurons across days reveals acute and persistent effects of psilocybin in the mouse brain
items.abstract: The psychedelic psilocybin offers a novel approach to treat depression and other psychiatric disorders. A single dose of psilocybin induces rapid neuroplastic effects that persist for many weeks to months. However, psilocybin's effect on neural firing beyond its systemic presence, and the neural mechanisms linking these acute and sustained effects remain unknown. Using chronically implanted Neuropixels probes, we tracked 1,692 neurons spanning prefrontal and hippocampal regions following saline and psilocybin injections and 24 h later. Psilocybin bidirectionally modulated firing acutely in a cell-type and region-specific manner. Persistent firing (24 h post-injection) is net suppressed relative to saline, including in acutely activated neurons. The late acute response, but not early peak response, predicted a neuron's firing 24 h later. To our knowledge, this is the first evidence that directly reveals psilocybin's sustained impacts on neuronal firing, providing key insight into the circuitry accompanying its lasting cognitive and behavioral alterations.

items.title: Motor cortex facilitates visual action override through the superior colliculus
items.corresponding_institution: Instituto de Neurociencias CSIC-UMH, San Juan de Alicante, Spain
items.abstract: Unexpected visual events can leave goal pursuit undisturbed or trigger visual action override - an interruption that redirects behaviour towards the stimulus. Using a visual distraction task in freely moving mice, population calcium recordings and causal perturbations identified the lateral motor-related superior colliculus (lSCm) as a key node controlling distractor engagement. Retinal inputs to the sensory-related SC signalled distractors even when mice ignored them. Pre-distractor behaviour and motor cortical activity predicted subsequent engagement, while increased corticocollicular and decreased nigrocollicular activity before distractor onset were consistent with a permissive state for override. Suppressing corticocollicular transmission weakened override without detectably altering task engagement. Single-unit recordings in head-fixed mice revealed response amplification in subsets of lSCm neurons during combined retinal and motor cortical stimulation, despite weak responses to either input alone. Motor cortical input thus facilitates sensory recruitment of collicular action circuits, shaping the balance between action stability and action override during ongoing goal pursuit.

items.title: Inter-protocol reproducibility of multi-shell diffusion MRI metrics across major neuroimaging study protocols
items.corresponding_institution: Center for Biomedical Imaging, Department of Radiology, New York University Grossman School of Medicine, New York, New York, USA.
items.abstract: Diffusion MRI is a core component of large-scale neuroimaging initiatives, yet the reproducibility of quantitative dMRI metrics across different acquisition protocols remains unclear. We acquired seven multi-shell diffusion protocols representative of major consortia and clinical settings on a single scanner in 41 healthy adults, isolating protocol effects from hardware and site variability. A linear mixed-effects model was used to estimate the inter-protocol coefficient of variation (CV) and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI), and standard model imaging (SMI) metrics across atlas-based white matter regions. Rank agreement was assessed with Kendall's W, and repeated scans of one protocol provided a reference for test-retest variability. Overall, inter-protocol variability was low, with median CVs of 2.9-6.1% for DTI, 3.7-5.0% for DKI, and 3.0-4.7% for SMI metrics. Protocols ranked subjects consistently (W = 0.73-0.86) but agreed less in absolute value (ICC = 0.31-0.66), with fractional anisotropy (FA) being the most stable metric. Acquisition parameters, including TE, b-values, and signal-to-noise ratio jointly explained 53-93% of the inter-protocol variance. Differences in the b-values used for DTI and DKI estimation were particularly important for the diffusivities: matching b-values across protocols reduced the median inter-protocol CV for MD from 5.0% to 1.8%, with smaller reductions for mean kurtosis (MK), axial kurtosis (AK) and the axonal water fraction (f). These findings demonstrate good reproducibility of quantitative higher-order diffusion MRI metrics across commonly used multi-shell acquisition protocols, which can be further improved by aligning b-values, providing a foundation for data pooling, harmonization, and normative modeling in large-scale neuroimaging studies.

items.title: State-dependent gating of sensory and cortical inputs by median raphe neurons
items.abstract: The mesopontine median raphe (MnR) plays an important role in regulating brain states, hippocampal network activity, and memory processes. Recent studies have revealed that the MnR comprises three major neuronal populations: serotonergic (5-HT), glutamatergic (Vglut3-expressing), and GABAergic neurons. How these distinct neuronal populations may gate sensory and cortical inputs across different brain states remains largely unknown. Here, we combined in vivo electrophysiological recording, sensory or optogenetic stimulation, and transgenic approaches to characterize the response properties of 5-HT, Vglut3, and GABAergic MnR neurons during wakefulness and sleep. We found that MnR neurons exhibited pronounced state-dependent responses to both sensory and cortical stimulation, with response amplitudes significantly greater during slow-wave sleep than during wakefulness. Auditory and somatosensory stimuli elicited fast responses in the MnR: 5-HT neurons were primarily suppressed, whereas Vglut3 and GABAergic neurons were primarily activated, suggesting the presence of direct inputs from sensory thalamic or brainstem structures. Retrograde tracing identified several brainstem structures and, notably, the medial prefrontal cortex as sources of direct projections to the MnR. Optogenetic stimulation of prefrontal inputs to the MnR evoked inhibition of 5-HT neurons but robust excitation of Vglut3 neurons during slow-wave sleep, suggesting top-down control of MnR activity by the prefrontal cortex. Together, these findings reveal that the MnR exhibits enhanced sensitivity to both ascending sensory and descending cortical inputs during sleep, suggesting that it may integrate environmental and cortical signals to regulate hippocampal network activity and gate sleep-dependent memory processing.

items.title: A four-dimensional single-cell and spatial atlas of cAMP-driven repair after rat spinal cord injury
items.corresponding_institution: Institute for Integrative Systems Biology (I2SysBio), CSIC-Universitat de Valencia, Paterna, Spain
items.abstract: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) induction through photoactivatable adenylate cyclase (bPAC) in corticospinal neurons enhances locomotion after spinal cord injury (SCI); however, the molecular and cellular mechanisms that underlie this improvement are unknown. Here we perform single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST) of spinal cord sections at the injury site of dorsal hemisected rats, to identify the pathways through which bPAC stimulation exerts its regenerative cues after SCI, along with the changes in cellular populations that occur in different parts of the spinal cord.

items.title: An isogenic human stem cell model reveals NGLY1-dependent control of microglial development
items.abstract: NGLY1 is a cytosolic N-glycanase involved in glycoprotein quality control and proteasome-mediated protein degradation and is critical for normal brain development and function. Although neuronal alterations caused by NGLY1 deficiency have been extensively characterized in animal and human cell models, how NGLY1 deficiency affects human glial cells, particularly microglia, the brain-resident innate immune cells, remains largely unknown. Using patient-derived NGLY1-deficient human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) lines and their corresponding CRISPR-mediated gene-corrected isogenic lines, we found that NGLY1-deficient primitive macrophage progenitors (PMPs) exhibited increased GlcNAc-Asn (GNA) accumulation and elevated expression of RUNX1, a key transcription factor regulating myeloid lineage development, accompanied by abnormal proliferation. Following further differentiation, NGLY1-deficient human microglia exhibited reduced morphological complexity and impaired phagocytic capacity. In addition, NGLY1-deficient microglia showed increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-1{beta}, IL-6, and TNF, under both basal and stimulated conditions, indicative of a heightened inflammatory state. Mechanistically, our data showed that RUNX1 upregulation induced by NGLY1 deficiency partially mediated impaired PMP proliferation and subsequent microglial abnormalities, implicating RUNX1 dysregulation in NGLY1-associated microglial dysfunction and identifying RUNX1 as a potential therapeutic target. Together, using patient-derived and gene-corrected isogenic hiPSCs, our study establishes a human stem cell platform for modeling NGLY1 deficiency and reveals that impaired deglycosylation alters human microglial developmental trajectories and ultimately compromises microglial homeostasis and function. These microglial abnormalities may contribute to the neurological deficits observed in patients carrying loss-of-function variants in NGLY1.

items.title: Age-dependent changes in the putamen transcriptome and proteome of a transgenic minipig model of Huntington's disease
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Animal Physiology and Genetics, Czech Academy of Sciences
items.abstract: Huntington's disease is an inherited neurodegenerative disorder with no disease-modifying treatment available. Preclinical trials of gene therapies rely on large animal models and the transgenic Huntington's disease (TgHD) minipig is one of them. Minipigs live more than a decade, so the effect of a single dose of gene therapy can be followed for years. The TgHD transgene carries a mixed CAG/CAA repeat that is not expected to expand somatically. However, its putamen, part of the striatum that degenerates first in patients, had not been examined by genome-wide methods, nor beyond 4 years of age. We compared the putamen of transgenic and wild-type minipigs at 4 and 8 years by RNA sequencing and label-free mass spectrometry proteomics, and measured mutant huntingtin by immunoassay. Seven genes were differentially expressed at 4 years and 3,324 at 8 years, and the pathway changes of the transcriptome and the proteome were concordant at that age. The D2 medium spiny neuron marker gene set was reduced at 8 years in both the transcriptome and the proteome. Mitochondrial and oxidative phosphorylation pathways were positively enriched at 4 years and negatively enriched at 8 years. Immune and complement pathways were positively enriched at 8 years, and the number of altered splicing events increased almost fivefold between 4 and 8 years. We detected no age-dependent accumulation of soluble mutant huntingtin. Since the repeat does not expand, these changes developed without somatic expansion, a major driver of progression in human Huntington's disease. We propose that the reduced neuronal markers reflect a loss of neuronal identity rather than neuronal death. The TgHD minipig would then recapitulate the slow early phase of the disease, when treatment is arguably most likely to help.

items.title: Waveform morphology links local circuit kinetics to cortical interactions
items.abstract: How does local cortical physiology shape interactions between brain regions? We combined neural mass modelling with human and macaque intracranial recordings to examine how synaptic kinetics link oscillatory waveform morphology to cortical interactions. In a modified excitatory-inhibitory Wilson-Cowan model, synaptic rise and decay kinetics shaped waveform geometry and phase-dependent responsiveness. Local kinetics and coupling symmetry jointly influenced interaction measures and temporal irreversibility, while phase-locked perturbations altered imaginary coherency and bivariate irreversibility even when the coupling strengths remained fixed. In stereo-EEG from 23 patients, waveform asymmetry was most strongly associated with local irreversibility, whereas mean instantaneous alpha frequency showed stronger associations with interregional measures. Subdural macaque electrocorticography reproduced the frequency associations but not the local waveform association. Together, these findings show that waveform shape carries information about local neuronal dynamics, provide a mechanistic framework for interpreting cortical interactions, and motivate testing waveform morphology as a guide to stimulation timing.

items.title: Macaque Vγ4+ γδ T cells exhibit distinct IFN-γ and IL-22 effector profiles that are dysregulated during chronic SIV infection and diarrheal disease
items.abstract: V{gamma}4+ {gamma}{delta} T cells contribute to colonic homeostasis in humans, but their biology in nonhuman primates remains poorly defined. Here, we characterized V{gamma}4+ {gamma}{delta} T cells in blood and intestinal tissues of healthy, diarrhea-inflicted, and SIV-infected rhesus macaques. TRG/TRD repertoire sequencing across colon, mesenteric lymph node, blood, and spleen revealed compartment-specific clonal architecture and colonic enrichment of TRGV3. Flow cytometric profiling revealed circulating and colonic V{gamma}4+ T cells were predominantly V{delta}1+, exhibited an effector memory phenotype, and displayed T-bet-dominant transcriptional profiles. High-dimensional clustering confirmed V{gamma}4+V{delta}1+ T cells as a distinct terminally differentiated lineage. Functionally, stimulated V{gamma}4+ T cells exhibited robust Th1/Th17 cytokine production, supporting dual inflammatory and barrier-protective roles. Campylobacter-associated diarrhea was characterized by mucosal expansion of central memory V{gamma}4+ T cells and altered cytokine responses. In contrast, ART-suppressed chronic SIV infection was associated with colonic enrichment of naive-like V{gamma}4+ T cells and increased ROR{gamma}t expression, alongside profound systemic loss of cytokine production but relative preservation of mucosal Th17-type responses. Both conditions exhibited a convergent loss of systemic Type 1 effector V{gamma}4+ T-cell responses, pointing to a shared functional alteration during chronic intestinal inflammation. Overall, these findings reveal disease-specific remodeling of V{gamma}4+ T cells during chronic intestinal inflammation and gut barrier disruption in chronic enterocolitis and SIV infection.

items.title: Direct Sputum Sequencing Reveals Mycobacterium tuberculosis Diversity Underrepresented by Culture in a High TB-Burden Setting
items.abstract: Background: Whole-genome sequencing of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) commonly relies on culture-derived isolates, potentially altering the bacterial populations represented. Direct sputum whole-genome sequencing (dsWGS) may better capture lineage composition and within-host variant diversity. Methods: We compared targeted-enrichment dsWGS with WGS of matched culture-derived isolates from participants initiating treatment for rifampicin-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis in Worcester, South Africa. We assessed sequencing performance, technical reproducibility, sputum-sampling variability, lineage and variant concordance, and resistance-associated variation, and explored associations with baseline clinical characteristics and treatment response. Results: Of 218 clinical dsWGS reactions, 139 passed sequencing quality criteria, yielding 113 eligible baseline sputum-culture pairs. Mixed-lineage infection was detected in 72/113 (63.7%) sputum specimens versus 7/113 (6.2%) matched cultures; 66/113 (58.4%) pairs showed reduced lineage diversity following culture. Permutation analysis indicated preferential retention of Lineage 2 and depletion of Lineage 3 after culture. Technical replicates preserved dominant phylotype assignments (median SNP Jaccard similarity 0.863), while independently collected sputum specimens showed greater variability. Among 38 concordant single-lineage pairs, 35,540/38,311 (92.8%) pair-specific variant observations were shared after filtering and raw-read recovery, while 2,497 (6.5%) were sputum-unique and 274 (0.7%) culture-unique. Discordance was concentrated among variable variants; 88.0% of shared variants variable in at least one specimen had higher allele frequencies in culture. No sputum-unique WHO Grade 1 or 2 resistance-associated mutations were identified in the strain-controlled subset, whereas eight mixed-lineage sputum samples versus three matched cultures harboured such mutations. Higher baseline low-frequency variant burden showed non-significant trends towards delayed culture conversion (log-rank p=0.144) and unfavourable treatment outcomes (log-rank p=0.400). Conclusions: Direct-sputum WGS revealed M. tuberculosis lineage and low-frequency variant diversity that was not fully represented by matched culture-derived genomes, despite high overall genomic concordance. These findings highlight the complementary value of direct-sputum sequencing for characterising within-host diversity, while suggesting that the representation of bacterial populations following culture may vary across epidemiological settings. Further research is needed to improve the accuracy of minority-variant detection and establish the clinical relevance of diversity measured directly from sputum.

items.title: SIRT3 preserves mitochondrial DNA integrity to restrain cGAS-STING signaling and autoimmune inflammation
items.abstract: Mitochondria play critical roles beyond energy production, including regulation of innate immunity through release of damage-associated molecular patterns such as mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). Sirtuin 3 (SIRT3), a mitochondrial deacetylase, modulates mitochondrial function, reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, and inflammation. Here, we investigate the role of SIRT3 in controlling Type I interferon (IFN) responses in macrophages. We show that Sirt3 depletion in mouse macrophages increases basal mtDNA release into the cytosol, activating the cGAS-STING pathway and enhancing the expression of IFN-{beta} and downstream interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs). Accordingly, Sirt3-deficient cells exhibit markedly increased resistance to vesicular stomatitis virus infection. Secreted IFN-{beta} also acts in a paracrine manner, priming neighboring cells and reinforcing antiviral defenses. Using mtDNA-deficient ({rho}0) cells, we demonstrate that intact mtDNA is essential for this amplified interferon response, as mtDNA depletion abolishes IFN-{beta} induction following Sirt3 knockdown. Mechanistically, increased mitochondrial ROS (mtROS) in SIRT3-deficient cells promotes mtDNA leakage and cGAS-STING activation, effects that are attenuated by the mitochondrial superoxide scavenger MitoTEMPO. In vivo, SIRT3 protects against chlorhexidine gluconate-induced peritoneal fibrosis by restraining macrophage infiltration, ISGs expression and fibrotic remodeling, underscoring its role in modulating STING-dependent inflammation and tissue damage. Finally, reanalysis of transcriptomic datasets from patients with lupus nephritis and rheumatoid arthritis reveals reduced SIRT3 expression, suggesting that SIRT3 downregulation is also associated with human inflammatory diseases. Collectively, our findings identify SIRT3 as an important regulator of mitochondrial integrity and oxidative stress that modulates innate immune and antiviral responses.

items.title: Structural basis for reprogramming group II intron target specificity
items.abstract: Group II introns are mobile ribozymes that, with their intron-encoded protein (IEP), insert into duplex DNA without a double-strand break, a route to programmed gene insertion so far confined to bacteria. How class IIA complexes recognize and remodel duplex DNA was unknown. We identify group IIA intron/IEP pairs that retrohome efficiently into linear, relaxed duplex DNA, and report cryo-EM structures of one, Voyager-1, at successive stages of insertion. Major- and minor-groove peptides clamp the 5' target and prime melting; intron nucleotides capture one strand; and a peptide linker threads between the re-annealing strands, reading 3' sequence and trapping the HNH nuclease in a nicking-competent position. Guided by these structures, we reprogram protein-encoded specificity, yielding combined RNA and protein-encoded recognition sufficient, by sequence, for single-site targeting in complex plant and animal genomes. Voyager-1 functions when formed in mammalian cells without Mg supplementation, overcoming a long-standing barrier to class IIA introns in eukaryotes.

items.title: Distinct contributions of cohesin-STAG1 and cohesin-STAG2 to the pluripotent and totipotent states
items.abstract: Cohesin organizes the three-dimensional genome and thereby regulates gene expression. In somatic cells, cohesin complexes carry either STAG1 or STAG2, paralogs that impart distinct chromatin binding dynamics and are both essential for mouse embryonic development. How each variant contributes to the maintenance and transitions of pluripotent cell state remains poorly understood. Using degrons and knockout clones in mouse embryonic stem cells, we show that neither STAG1 nor STAG2 is individually required for differentiation towards primitive endoderm or for transitions between ground-state and metastable pluripotency. Nonetheless, STAG2 is necessary to support naive pluripotency in the metastable but not in the ground-state. Depletion of either STAG protein upregulates totipotency-associated transcripts, yet an increased proportion of two-cell-like cells is only observed upon STAG1 loss. These findings suggest complementary roles for the two cohesin variants in stabilizing the pluripotent state. While cohesin-STAG1 prevents return to totipotency, cohesin-STAG2 restrains exit towards commitment.

items.title: RBM15::MKL1 uncouples SPOC-dependent m6A remodeling from WTAP recruitment
items.abstract: The recurrent t(1;22) translocation associated with pediatric acute megakaryoblastic leukemia generates the RBM15::MKL1 (RM) fusion protein that retains the RNA-binding and SPOC domains of RBM15. RBM15 recruits the N6-methyladenosine (m6A) methyltransferase complex (MTC), of which WTAP is a key regulatory component. How RM engages this machinery and whether the SPOC domain is required for its leukemogenic activity remain unclear. Here, we investigated the molecular determinants of WTAP recruitment by RBM15 and RM and their contribution to RM-mediated disruption of megakaryocyte differentiation. Structure-guided mutagenesis identified a conserved basic surface within the isolated RBM15 SPOC domain that is required for WTAP association. Unexpectedly, disruption of this surface or complete SPOC deletion failed to abolish WTAP association with full-length RBM15 or RM, indicating that additional determinants mediate MTC recruitment. In human erythroleukemia cells, RM impaired TPA-induced megakaryocytic maturation, as assessed by differentiation markers, polyploidization, and morphology; this blockade persisted following SPOC disruption. However, transcriptomic analysis demonstrated that RM lacking the SPOC domain elicited an attenuated gene expression response compared with unmutated RM, including alterations in WNT/Beta-catenin-associated genes. m6A-enriched RNA profiling further revealed extensive remodeling of the m6A epitranscriptome by RM, while SPOC deletion shifted RM-associated m6A changes toward a more wild-type-like state. Together, these findings demonstrate that although the SPOC domain contributes to RM-mediated molecular regulation, it is dispensable for stable MTC association and maintenance of the differentiation blockade, revealing previously unrecognized redundancy in RBM15-mediated recruitment of the m6A machinery.

items.title: Minimal, synthetic arginine deiminase pathway provides full ATP demand for cellular growth
items.abstract: Bottom-up construction of synthetic cells requires a simple, yet robust ATP-generating system. The arginine deiminase (ADI) pathway offers a minimal, enzyme-based alternative to more complex ATP-producing systems such as glycolytic routes, respiratory chains or photosystems. Here, we implement the ADI pathway in Escherichia coli and test its capacity to fully replace native ATP generation. First, we designed and tested synthetic ADI operons through combinatorial library screening and selected high-performing variants. Using the best performing-ADI variant, we progressively reduced the cells dependence on native ATP generation while increasing selection for ADI-dependent growth through targeted knockout strains and growth conditions, followed by adaptive laboratory evolution. This resulted in a strain in which the ADI pathway sustained growth in minimal medium at a doubling time of 21 hours, serving as the sole source of ATP. Whole-genome sequencing of evolved strains revealed that this transition required loss-of-function mutations in the native respiratory chain. These findings demonstrate that the ATP supply of a cell can be fully supported by the ADI pathway, which has not been demonstrated in nature. Moreover, the ability of the pathway to sustain growth with a relatively high growth rate highlights its potential to fully power synthetic cells and support other biotechnological applications.

items.title: MYC coordinates tRNA pool expansion during re-entry into proliferation by promoting pre-tRNA maturation
items.abstract: Re-entry into proliferation requires rapid expansion of the translational machinery to support cell growth. How cells replenish abundant, long-lived tRNAs remains unclear. Increased RNA polymerase III activity can lead to accumulation of pre-tRNAs without proportional expansion of mature pools, suggesting that transcription alone may be insufficient. Using differentiated HepaRG cells undergoing re-entry into proliferation, we quantified precursor and mature tRNA dynamics. While the total tRNA pool expanded with cell number, mature tRNA abundance per cell remained stable, accompanied by lower precursor-to-mature ratios and accelerated precursor turnover, consistent with enhanced maturation. MYC depletion impaired precursor turnover and compromised maintenance of mature tRNAs and their processing machinery. Across distinct proliferative transitions, the magnitude of per-cell tRNA accumulation paralleled changes in processing-factor mRNA and protein abundance, with both responses dependent on MYC. These findings identify MYC-dependent coordination of tRNA production and maturation as a mechanism supporting the distinct biosynthetic demands of proliferative transitions.

items.title: Selective ultrasonic suppression of pathological brain hyperactivity via an endogenous CAV3-NCX1 axis
items.abstract: Selective suppression of pathological hyperactivity is a major therapeutic challenge across brain disorders. Ultrasound stimulation can modulate neural activity, yet the molecular basis of its inhibitory effects and its ability to selectively inhibit hyperactive rather than basally active cells remain unclear. Here, we identify the caveolin-3 (CAV3)-sodium-calcium exchanger-1 (NCX1) complex as a previously unknown mediator of state-dependent ultrasound-induced neural inhibition. Prolonged ultra-low-intensity ultrasound stimulation engages NCX1-mediated Ca2+ extrusion in hyperactive neurons and astrocytes, sparing cells with basal activity. NCX1 is both necessary and sufficient for this inhibitory response, and disruption of the CAV3-NCX1 interface abolishes the ultrasound-induced effects. In vivo, targeted ultrasound stimulation suppresses fear-evoked hyperactivity and freezing in an NCX1-dependent manner and attenuates neuropathic pain-associated hyperactivity, allodynia, and hippocampal epileptiform activity. These findings establish a molecular mechanism for state-dependent ultrasound inhibition, providing a basis for a new approach to neuromodulation that selectively targets pathological hyperactivity.

items.title: Antibody design across observed and forecasted antigenic evolution
items.abstract: The therapeutic efficacy of antibodies is often limited by the evolution of their targets. Designing or eliciting antibodies that withstand such evolution is challenging as their binding interfaces must accommodate antigenic variation. Here, we introduce Germinal Multi, a computational framework for de novo antibody design and rescue that jointly optimizes a single paratope against multiple antigenic variants. We applied Germinal Multi to cancer and viral antigens, targeting both observed antigenic variation and prospective antibody escape. Multi-target optimization yielded antibodies that bound resistance-associated EGFR variants or that neutralized antigenically distinct historical SARS-CoV-2 variants, with recognition extending to variants withheld from the design process. Beyond acting on observed evolution, we redesigned the broadly neutralizing antibody BD55-1205 to restore neutralization of a prospective escape variant engineered with guidance from an evolutionary forecasting model, while preserving activity against the parental variant. Successful candidates were identified after screening tens of designs per campaign. Together, these results establish multi-target computational design as a strategy for generating antibody breadth across observed antigenic variation and demonstrate the potential of evolutionary forecasting to guide antibody redesign against prospective escape.

items.title: Language-guided domain adaptation improves protein sequence representations for antimicrobial resistance analysis
items.corresponding_institution: Beijing Institute of Genomics, Chinese Academy of Sciences
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in bacterial pathogens complicates infectious disease management. Protein sequences encode molecular features underlying resistance functions such as antibiotic inactivation and drug efflux, providing a basis for investigating bacterial AMR. Protein language models can extract transferable representations from these sequences. However, general purpose protein language models have limited capacity to represent AMR-associated sequences, while task-specific tools often address individual prediction problems. These limitations highlight the need for protein representations that better capture resistance associated functions and can be reused across complementary tasks, supporting systematic AMR analysis from sequence variation to functional relationships among proteins. We developed BacLLM, a language-guided protein representation framework that integrates annotation derived functional knowledge into protein language model representations for AMR analysis in bacterial pathogens. Through sequence enhancement, semantic enrichment of UniProt annotations, and cross modal contrastive learning, BacLLM transfers LLM encoded annotation priors into the sequence encoder, enabling sequence only inference after training. Compared with baseline models, BacLLM provided more informative representations of resistance associated sequences, achieving a mean F1 score of 0.956 across six AMR benchmarks with logistic regression, 2.7 percentage points above the strongest baseline. It also captured resistance associated mutational signals at single residue resolution and preserved taxonomic relationships not reflected by phenotype based clinical groupings. Moreover, BacLLM recovered resistance associated functional organization within a TolC centered protein association network, prioritizing proteins with low sequence identity to TolC but predicted structural similarity to TolC. Extending the same representation framework to an intervention oriented application, BacLLM also improved strain level phage host matching for phage therapy candidate prioritization. Together, these findings establish BacLLM as a reusable protein representation framework for analyzing resistance associated sequence variation and functional organization, with applications in AMR surveillance and phage candidate prioritization.

items.title: Local GEBVs and additive variance in maize heterotic groups across low- and high-stress environments
items.abstract: Hybrid maize (Zea mays L.) parents are chosen within heterotic groups. Drought and heat stress are expected to become more frequent, but little is known about how they change the additive variance of each group and where in the genome it lies. We analyzed testcross grain yield from 62 Genomes to Fields environments, classified as low or high stress by climate. For 1,362 parents from three heterotic groups and two doubled-haploid families, we fitted a genomic model with group deviations and calculated local genomic estimated breeding values in 164-kb segments. In the heterotic groups, high stress reduced additive variance by 4057%, and the genetic correlation between conditions was 0.730.99. Within groups, the distribution of variance across the genome was similar between conditions (correlation 0.841.00), and genotype-by-environment interaction was spread over many low-variance segments. Genome-wide association detected 25 loci under low stress and 18 under high stress, none shared, but half or more lay in high-effect, high-variance segments that were nearly the same in both conditions. The best possible cross between the two heterotic pools exceeded the best evaluated hybrid by 105117%, a gap that depended on segment size, not on stress. With 25 founders, stacking the best segments reached 9495% of the pool potential, versus 5692% for selection on total breeding value, whose founders were more related. Founders chosen in one condition reached, in the other, 94100% of the potential of those chosen there. Local breeding values can guide the choice of donors and founders under both conditions.

items.title: Prediction Dynamically Modulates Gain and Width of Population Frequency Tuning in Human Auditory Cortex
items.abstract: During perception, the brain must veridically portray sensory representations while simultaneously highlighting unexpected events. According to two-process theory of predictive perception, this balance is achieved via complementary mechanisms: precision-weighted predictions sharpen sensory tuning around expected features, while momentary surprisal scales response gain, dampening expected inputs and amplifying unexpected violations. However, standard approaches to investigate these processes, such as categorical multivariate decoding, primarily capture shifts in overall signal-to-noise, making it difficult to disentangle changes in population tuning width from modulations in response gain. Here, we combine ultra-high-field functional magnetic resonance imaging (7T fMRI) with population receptive field (pRF) modelling and a continuous Bayesian ideal observer to test how expectations dynamically modulate frequency tuning across the human auditory hierarchy. We first established static pRF preferences and tuning widths independently of predictive inference. We then separately compared this static pRF tuning against two dynamically modulated alternatives. The first model evaluated how tone-by-tone precision-weighted predictions dynamically sharpen and broaden pRF tuning width, while the second model evaluated how gain (by amplification and dampening) was modulated by tone-by-tone information-theoretic surprisal. Across primary, belt, and associative auditory cortices, both a sharpening model driven by precision-weighted predictions and a gain model driven by surprisal explained significantly more variance compared to a static baseline model. Counterfactual models inverting these driving features yielded no improvement, ruling out non-specific model mimicry. Additionally, contrasting local and global tonotopic implementations revealed a feature-selective dissociation: whereas precision-weighted predictions locally sharpened pRFs tuned to expected frequencies, surprisal acted as a global broadcast signal that multiplicatively scaled pRF gain across all frequency channels of the tonotopic map. Together, these findings demonstrate that the auditory system continuously balances selectivity for expected structure and responsiveness to surprising input through local sharpening and global gain modulation.

items.title: Spatial Transcriptomics Reveals Age-Specific Cancer Hallmark Architecture in Pediatric and Adult Brain Tumors
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biology, Brigham Young University, Provo, UT, 84061, USA
items.abstract: Pediatric cancers are fundamentally different from their adult counterparts. Specifically, pediatric cancers carry fewer mutations, interact with developing immune systems, and have active developmental microenvironments. The tumor microenvironment (TME), which includes the surrounding stromal cells, immune cells, blood vessels, and extracellular matrix, plays a crucial role in cancer progression, metastasis, behavior, and treatment response. To better understand the effects of the pediatric tumor microenvironment on tumor gene expression, we acquired spatial transcriptomic data from 17 pediatric brain tumor samples and analyzed it through a Cancer Hallmarks framework. Cancer Hallmarks, as outlined by Hanahan and Weinberg, provide a comprehensive set of 14 biological capabilities that cancers acquire to enable tumor growth and metastasis. We compared the spatial gene expression patterns of the Cancer Hallmarks gene sets between the TME and neoplastic compartments in pediatric brain tumors. Compared with a similar study of adult brain tumors, in which Cancer Hallmark expression patterns clearly separated the TME and neoplastic compartments, we identified three hallmarks ("Deregulating Cellular Energetics," "Senescent Cells," and "Evading Growth Suppressors") whose predominant cellular compartments differed between pediatric and adult tumors. In pediatric samples, these hallmarks were associated primarily with the TME rather than the neoplastic compartment. This shift implicates an age-specific rewiring of the tumor ecosystem. We also provide clear evidence of strong transcriptomic regulation in genes shared by pediatric and adult neoplastic compartments. Finally, we show how measures of spatial autocorrelation may be used to distinguish tumor grade.

items.title: Bidirectional acetate exchange couples ethanol turnover to acetyl-CoA metabolism in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
items.corresponding_institution: TBI, Université de Toulouse, CNRS, INRAE, INSA, Toulouse, France
items.abstract: Overflow metabolism describes the excretion of partially oxidized metabolites into the extracellular environment during rapid sugar utilization. Although these metabolites can later be reused, it remains unclear whether reassimilation also occurs during ongoing sugar consumption, and if so, how. Here, 13C-isotope tracing and metabolic flux analysis of acetate exchange in Saccharomyces cerevisiae during hexose utilization reveal that net acetate overflow is only the small difference between order-of-magnitude larger simultaneous excretion and assimilation fluxes. Unlike ethanol production, acetate exchange is not determined by hexose uptake but depends on metabolic processes downstream of glycolysis. Ethanol oxidation contributes to acetate excretion even during net ethanol production, directly linking the two main overflow pathways. We exploited this understanding to redirect extracellular acetate into the acetyl-CoA-derived product mevalonate. These results establish acetate overflow as a dynamic exchange linking ethanol turnover to acetyl-CoA metabolism, in which acetate is simultaneously an overflow product and a carbon source that can be redirected toward bioproduction.

items.title: N- and T-genes framework for pathway deregulation: Taxonomy, progression, and protection in cancer
items.corresponding_institution: Inst. de Cibernetica, Matematica y Fisica (ICIMAF)
items.abstract: Background. Pathway analysis is widely used to interpret gene expression, but conventional enrichment depends on arbitrary thresholds and does not quantify deregulation magnitude. Recent reformulations based on average log-fold changes remove the threshold but still average over all annotated genes, diluting the signal from the genes that actually drive the normal-to-tumor transition. The N/T framework, which identifies genes with exclusive expression intervals in normal (N) or tumor (T) samples, offers a selective alternative, but it had not been extended to pathway- level quantification, taxonomy, or cross-cancer comparison. Methods. We define effective activation frequencies for Reactome pathways based on N- and T-genes: for each sample and pathway, the effective N (T) frequency is the fraction of annotated N (T) genes active in a normal (tumor) sample. The analysis proceeds in three explicit steps: (i) cohort averages identify the pathways important in each tissue; (ii) averages over hierarchical-clustering groups, ordered by the number of active genes, reveal sequences of pathway activation and deactivation along progression; (iii) a minimum spanning tree (MST) built on pathway-frequency vectors -- independent of the number of active genes -- defines the molecular taxonomy, and branch averages identify subtype-specific programs. We apply the framework to the full set of Reactome pathways in prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC), and glioblastoma (GBM), analyzing both tumor and normal compartments. Results. In PRAD tumors (n=499), hierarchical clustering identifies four ordered progression groups and the MST resolves six main molecular subtypes comprising 406 tumors (81.4%): B1 (42.1%; MET/NFE2L2/energy metabolism), B2 (13.8%; RAS/apoptosis/telomere), and four smaller subtypes defined by PTEN (B3), DNA repair and lipid metabolism (B4), inflammation and LXR-mediated lipid metabolism (B5), and neuronal development and base excision repair (B6). An eight-gene perfect T panel reproduces the MST subtypes at gene level. Analysis of normal prostatic tissue (n=52) reveals a hierarchy of protection: immune response, apoptosis, and senescence are lost or partially lost early, DNA repair at an intermediate stage, and cell cycle regulation and receptor tyrosine kinase signaling last; an eleven-gene N panel reproduces this hierarchy at gene level. The cross-cancer comparison shows that this architecture is a general property: DNA repair, cell cycle, and RTK protection are maintained in normal tissue across PRAD, LUAD, LIHC, and GBM, while the specific pathways lost in normals and gained in tumors are tissue-specific (MET/NFE2L2 in PRAD; NTRK/LXR/phagosome in LIHC; surfactant/FGFR/glycosylation in LUAD; TP53loss/lipid metabolism/glycosylation in GBM). Taxonomic heterogeneity decreases from PRAD (six subtypes) to LIHC (two) to LUAD and GBM (one dominant program), paralleling an increase in the number of activated T-genes. Conclusions. The framework eliminates dilution by non-nformative genes, quantifies pathway deregulation sample by sample, and unifies tumor taxonomy with a molecular indicator of progression. Its most distinctive contribution is the joint analysis of normal and tumor compartments across cancer types, which links loss of protection in normal tissue to gain of progression programs in tumors and reveals both shared and tissue-specific cancer mechanisms. The method is general and applicable across cancer types, although quantitative results depend on the underlying cohort.

items.title: Personalized functional networks scale with brain size beyond anatomy and are altered in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome
items.abstract: Anatomically, cortical regions scale differentially with total brain size: some show disproportionate contraction in smaller brains and expansion in larger brains, while others show relative stability. Whether personalized functional networks (PFNs) follow similar areal scaling principles, and how these principles shape functional reorganization in conditions that alter brain size, remain unknown. We investigated PFN scaling in typical development (ages 8-23; n=1,332) and 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS), a neuropsychiatric genetic disorder with globally reduced brain size (62 cases, 153 matched controls; ages 10-24). In typical development, PFN scaling diverged from anatomy, deviating more from proportional scaling, particularly in association networks. In 22q11DS, accounting for expected scaling with brain size reduction revealed two robust network effects: relative peripheral visual reduction and relative cingulo-opercular enlargement. Vertex-level 22q11DS PFN reorganization beyond global cortical reduction showed spatial alignment with normative PFN changes associated with brain size, linking typical scaling principles to disorder-related alterations.

items.title: Confidence in global motion discrimination is better predicted by perceptual reliability than by stimulus-based heuristics
items.abstract: Decision-making requires evaluating the reliability of perceptual estimates, but whether confidence reflects perceptual reliability or stimulus-based heuristics remains debated. We used a multiple-aperture global motion stimulus in which the global direction, and therefore motion coherence, is only available after integrating locally ambiguous signals, so that no simple stimulus statistic can serve as a shortcut. Observers reported the global direction in two successive intervals and then chose which decision was more likely to be correct. Confidence tracked accuracy beyond what coherence alone could explain: observers were more accurate in chosen intervals even at the same coherence level. Observers also frequently reported the direction opposite to the true motion, and, in direct comparisons, were more confident in these errors than in other large errors. We compared two image-computable models of motion integration. A standard motion-energy model failed to produce opposite-direction errors and the associated confidence pattern. A normalized motion-energy model, adding tuned inhibition among direction channels and an untuned gain control that increases overall activation with coherence, accounted for most of the variance in both perceptual decisions and confidence judgments. Tuned inhibition, which must be sharp if it is close to excitation in strength, produced the opposite-direction errors and reproduced the direction of their confidence advantage, and the untuned gain was needed for confidence to depend on coherence as strongly as observed. Confidence was read out from the same signal as the perceptual decision, and noise at the confidence stage, although probably present, added little to the fit beyond explaining the accuracy difference between chosen and unchosen intervals. These results suggest that confidence in this task relies on perceptual reliability. They also suggest that seemingly unusual metacognitive behavior can emerge from perceptual computations, which must therefore be modeled explicitly to identify genuine confidence mechanisms.

items.title: Neurocognitive signatures of intrinsic motivation in naturalistic information seeking and memory
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Psychological Sciences, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA 47907
items.abstract: Humans often seek information without direct external reward. Theories distinguish two major dimensions of this intrinsic motivation: wanting, the desire to resolve an information gap, and liking, the enjoyment of the information itself. However, how these motivational dimensions shape self-guided information-seeking behavior, neural activity, and memory formation in realworld contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, we developed a naturalistic fMRI paradigm in which participants freely browsed the internet, subsequently recalled their browsing experiences, and retrospectively reported their moment-to-moment wanting and liking. We found that both dimensions predicted more stable browsing trajectories but engaged partially dissociable neural systems: wanting recruited regions supporting goal-directed cognition, whereas liking engaged affective regions. Wanting and liking also interacted to predict memory, with wanting predicting recall primarily when liking was low. Compared with active browsing, passive viewing of the same web content reduced wanting and liking and diminished their dissociation, yet both continued to predict memory and intersubject neural similarity in the default mode network. These findings show that naturally fluctuating wanting and liking guide how we seek and remember information through overlapping yet distinct neurocognitive mechanisms.

items.title: Acute hypertension causes focal coronary artery perivascular cGAS-, IRF3, and IFNAR-dependent type I interferon responses
items.abstract: Hypertension exposes coronary arteries to dynamic mechanical forces that alter the structural integrity and lead to pathologic changes such as aneurysm, dissection, or atherogenesis. Although the effects of chronic hypertension have been extensively studied, the early molecular responses to increased luminal pressure remain poorly understood. Here, we find that acute hypertension in murine coronary arteries induced by transverse aortic constriction (TAC) causes focal perivascular type I interferon (IFN) responses in the vessel wall in contrast to comparatively homogeneous perivascular fibrosis. Spatial transcriptomics and RNAscope independently demonstrate spatially clustered expression of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) in the walls of pressurized left and right coronary arteries in the first week after TAC. Genetic disruption of cGAS or IRF3 each markedly attenuated the perivascular ISG response, indicating the response is a consequence of DNA sensing. Pharmacologic disruption of type I IFN signaling using an anti-IFNAR antibody abolished pressure-induced induction of focal ISG expression suggesting the pathway can be inhibited therapeutically. Since focal type I IFN signaling in the infarct borderzone of the left ventricle increased risk of dilation and rupture, we propose that focal perivascular type I IFN signaling in the vessel wall may serve as a nidus for analogous pathologies like aneurysm, dissection, or atherogenesis and represent a potential target for therapy.

items.title: Prim-O-glucosylcimifugin suppresses M2 macrophage polarization via the JAK2-STAT6-PPARγ pathway to alleviate allergic asthma
items.corresponding_institution: Haikou Hospiatl of Traditional Chinese Medicine
items.abstract: Background: Allergic asthma (AA) is a chronic respiratory disease closely linked to immune-inflammatory responses driven by M2 macrophage polarization. PrimO-glucosylcimifugin (POG), a natural bioactive compound from Saposhnikovia divaricata (SD), alleviates inflammation in acute lung injury mice, but whether it mitigates AA by modulating M2 macrophage polarization remains unclear.
