We assessed harmonization effectiveness using covariate-adjusted intraclass correlation coefficients and site-level pairwise differences, and evaluated biological effect preservation using Hedges' g, regression coefficients, and statistical significance for comparisons between cognitively impaired and unimpaired participants. For imputed analyses, effect sizes and regression coefficients were pooled using Rubin's rules, with statistical inference based on the pooled estimates. Post-processing harmonization reduced site-level variability compared to the original data, with method performance varying across evaluation metrics, while overall harmonization quality remained comparable after MI. Disease group differences remained statistically significant across all combinations, exhibiting a consistent regional pattern, strongest in Braak I and weakest in Braak VI. MI modestly increased effect size and coefficient estimates, with improved precision reflected by median standard error ratios below 1 (0.89 for effect sizes and 0.93 for coefficients). These findings indicate that integrating MI with harmonization preserves disease group differences and improves statistical efficiency without compromising harmonization performance, supporting a practical framework for multisite neuroimaging studies.

items.title: Adaptation can explain cortical responses to sound deviance without requiring prediction
items.corresponding_institution: Institute for Behavioural Neuroscience, Dept. of Experimental Psychology, University College London
items.abstract: Sensory systems amplify what is rare, allowing animals to orient toward threats and opportunities hidden among regular events. Whether this deviance detection reflects neuronal adaptation or error against the brain's predictive model is debated. The two processes can contribute simultaneously because the context that enables prediction also drives adaptation. To dissociate them, we recorded from primary auditory cortex neurons in awake mice during a modified oddball paradigm that separated recent sound history from longer-term sequence statistics. Contextual effects ranged from suppression to facilitation of responses. Facilitation increased with deviance magnitude, as expected for prediction error. However, neither facilitation, suppression, nor stimulus-specific adaptation depended on these longer-term statistics. A normalization model in which a neuron's inputs adapt at different rates reproduced the range of contextual effects and their weakening in background noise. Adaptive normalization can therefore generate deviance signals, including facilitation, without requiring a predictive model.

items.title: Whole-mount three-dimensional imaging and quantitative analysis platform for early brain development using dorsal forebrain spheroids
items.abstract: Three-dimensional culture systems have emerged as a bridge between in vitro and in vivo models. Organoids and spheroids derived from human stem cells can model cellular interactions, morphology and organization of the neocortex, and provide a platform for future translational research into neurological disorders. However, the heterogeneity commonly found in 3D culture systems presents considerable challenges for identifying significant, reproducible, and disorder-relevant phenotypes. Here, we present a rigorous methodological framework for the longitudinal analysis of dorsal forebrain spheroids, beginning with gross spheroid morphology, extending to structural phenotypes in rosette morphogenesis, and culminating in cellular analyses of neural progenitor cell proliferation and cell cycle dynamics. This workflow integrates isogenic iPSC-derived spheroid culture, whole-mount optical clearing, high-resolution 3D imaging and reconstruction, and cumulative EdU-labeling assays. Testing the sensitivity of this approach in an isogenic Down syndrome model, we reliably detected new features of altered spheroid growth, delayed rosette emergence, reduced rosette density, and prolonged progenitor cell cycle progression. This approach provides a reproducible strategy for measuring complex developmental phenotypes in 3D culture models and can be applied to neurodevelopmentally altered cell lines beyond Down syndrome.

items.title: Whole-bulb LSFEM enables automated reconstruction and quantitative spatial mapping of thousands of olfactory glomeruli
items.corresponding_institution: University of Bonn Medical Faculty, IEECR
items.abstract: The glomerular layer of the olfactory bulb (OB) transforms chemical information into the first spatially organized neural representation of odor identity. Yet its three-dimensional architecture remains difficult to quantify at whole-bulb scale. Here, we establish an end-to-end framework integrating light-sheet fluorescence expansion microscopy (LSFEM) with automated reconstruction of thousands of individual glomeruli across intact mouse OBs. LSFEM preserves whole-bulb architecture and supports genetically encoded fluorescence and immunolabelling, providing continuous multichannel input for automated analysis. SegFormer-based segmentation of 2D optical sections was followed by morphology-guided separation and three-dimensional object reconstruction. Across 12 intact bulbs, the workflow yielded a median of 2,677 glomeruli per bulb, approaching the 2,851 reported by complete three-dimensional reconstruction. Object-level maps further revealed that glomeruli spanning a broad range of volumes were intermingled throughout the bulb without evident size-defined anatomical domains. Because each reconstructed glomerulus retains a three-dimensional centroid coordinate, the resulting object map can additionally be used as a specimen-specific spatial reference framework, allowing distances and distributions to be expressed relative to defined glomerular or anatomical positions within the intact OB. Together, whole-bulb LSFEM and automated reconstruction provide a scalable framework for quantitative three-dimensional mapping of glomerular number, morphology, and spatial organization, and the relative positioning of additional anatomical signals within the glomerular architecture.

items.title: Partial microglial depletion attenuates Purkinje cell degeneration and reshapes both glial and inflammatory responses in a mouse model of selective neurodegeneration
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Neuroscience of Castile and Leon, Universidad de Salamanca
items.abstract: Background The microglial population contributes to the inflammatory environment during neurodegeneration. Its role in neuronal loss remains hard to distinguish from its response to injury. We investigated how early pharmacological reduction of this population affects Purkinje cell preservation, behaviour and the cerebellar glial response. Methods We administered PLX5622 to Purkinje cell degeneration (PCD) and wild-type (WT) mice from postnatal day (P) 15 to P24 and compared them with their respective untreated controls. We assessed motor coordination, spontaneous behaviours and novel-object recognition at P17, P21 and P25. At P25, we quantified regional Purkinje cell preservation, glial immunoreactivity and microglial abundance and morphology. We assessed selected transcripts in whole-cerebellum samples by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). Results At P25, treated PCD mice showed better motor coordination, improvements in selected spontaneous behaviours and greater novel-object discrimination. Greater Purkinje cell preservation coincided with lower glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) immunoreactivity in lobes IV-V and VIII. Microglial density decreased in all four PCD regions analysed. The territory encompassed by the processes of residual microglia expanded in both genotypes. In PCD mice, CD68-positive tissue area decreased in lobes I-II and IV-V, and the proportion of Iba1-positive area occupied by CD68 decreased in IV-V. CD45, CD16/32 and CD206 immunoreactivity decreased alongside selective reductions in immune, inflammatory and phagocytosis-associated transcripts. Treated WT mice showed early behavioural changes, including reduced novel-object discrimination. Conclusions Early PLX5622 treatment can modify the outcome of genetically driven cerebellar degeneration in PCD mice. The benefits achieved with partial microglial depletion provide a preclinical rationale for testing how the timing and extent of glial modulation influence neuronal protection during active degeneration.

items.title: Social Connection: Resting-State Functional Connectivity Associations with Social Networks, and the Roles of Empathy and Sex
items.abstract: Smaller social networks (SNs) negatively influence cognition, psychiatric trajectories and mortality. Studies linking SNs to resting-state functional connectivity (FC) inconsistently suggest orbito-frontal and frontoparietal regions and implicate a potential role for empathy and sex. We investigate how SN characteristics relate to FC, additionally assessing if empathy and sex alter these associations. Group-independent component analysis was applied to multi-band resting-state fMRI from 83 participants (Caltech Conte dataset: ds003798). The Social Network Index measures SN-contacts (SN-contacts) SN-diversity (number of roles) and SN-embeddedness (number of contact groups) and the Empathy Quotient measured empathy. Using MANCOVA, we investigate if resting-state network power and connectivity are associated with SNI measures and whether these relationships differ by empathizing ability and sex. Participants aged 18-48 (mean age 29.3+/-7.0, 55% male) demonstrated SN-contacts and SN-diversity associated with lower frontal-pole FC within the default-mode network (DMN, q-values<0.05). Empathy altered how SN-diversity and SN-contacts relate to superior lateral-occipital, default mode and salience network FC (q-values<0.05). Finally, males and females showed diverging associations of SN-contacts and SN-diversity with salience network power. Smaller SNs were associated with increased anterior-DMN FC, potentially indicating a tendency towards internally-directed cognition in more socially isolated individuals. Opposing relationships between SNs with salience and lateral-frontoparietal networks by empathy level highlights empathy as critical for understanding social biology. Males and females differed in SN associations with salience network coherency, supporting known sex-specific neural correlates of social behavior. These findings provide insights into the biology of social networks, offering potential targets for studying social deficits in psychiatric populations.

items.title: GFP-Tel1 is a marker of reversed replication forks that reveals constant fork backtracking during deoxyribonucleotide imbalance
items.corresponding_institution: Centre de Recherche en Biologie cellulaire de Montpellier (CRBM), Université de Montpellier-Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique
items.abstract: The apical kinase of the DNA Damage Response Tel1/ATM participates in at least three transactions key to the preservation of genome integrity: maintenance of a homeostatic telomere length, signaling of double strand breaks (DSB) in the DNA and a yet-poorly-defined contribution at reversed forks, a structure arising during problems in DNA replication. In a previous work, by tagging Tel1 in its N-terminus with yeast Enhanced Green Fluorescent Protein, we discovered that Tel1 forms foci in close proximity to the nuclear periphery in response to both chemically and enzymatically induced DSB. Here, we explore the determinants of this localization to the nuclear envelope, and we uncover that the subnuclear localization of the foci are a discriminant feature of Tel1's roles: foci forming in the interior of the nucleus mark reversed replication forks. In contrast, Tel1's function at telomeres are not tractable using GFP-Tel1 as a tool. Importantly, and in contrast to the prevalent notion that fork reversal is a phenomenon greatly restricted to metazoan replication forks, our characterization in the yeast S. cerevisiae of GFP-Tel1 at reversed forks allows us to propose a reconciling principle for how fork reversal contributes to tolerating replicative stress across evolutionary distant organisms.

items.title: A harmonized functional reference framework for GBA1
items.abstract: Systematic functional evidence is lacking for most rare GBA1 variants, limiting their interpretation in Gaucher disease (GD) and Parkinsons disease (PD). Here, we used a multiplexed assay of variant effect (MAVE) to generate a comprehensive atlas of lysosome-specific glucocerebrosidase (GCase) activity for more than 10400 GBA1 variants, covering 97 percent of all possible single-amino-acid substitutions. The atlas recapitulated known structural and biochemical determinants of glucocerebrosidase function and revealed concordance between functional impairment and expert-curated pathogenicity classifications. It identified significantly reduced activity in 94 of 186 reported variants of uncertain significance and revealed a quantitative relationship between functional impairment and GD disease severity. Integration with the Global PD Genetics Program associated greater variant-level functional impairment with earlier PD onset and higher PD odds ratios. Independent measurements of lysosomal glucocerebrosidase activity in stable cell lines expressing individual variants validated the MAVE results and resolved subtle functional deficits among variants close to the wild-type range, including established PD risk alleles. These findings provide a functional reference framework linking GBA1 variants to their molecular consequences and clinical phenotypes and demonstrate how comprehensive variant-effect maps can inform genetic interpretation and precision medicine.

items.title: Brain disorder mechanisms and therapeutic targets identified from developmental, cell-specific gene regulation
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Developmental and Regenerative Medicine, University of Oxford, OX3 7TY ; Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, UCSF; Weill Institute fo
items.abstract: Genetic variation influences brain physiology and disease across cell types and development. We integrated whole-genome sequencing, bulk RNA sequencing, and single-nucleus multiome profiling from 231 human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex donors spanning six postconceptional weeks to 92 years. Across 24 brain-related traits, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric genetic risk was enriched in neuronal transcriptomic and chromatin profiles, whereas neurodegenerative risk was enriched in microglia. Thousands of expression, chromatin accessibility, and splicing quantitative trait loci revealed developmental and cell-type-specific regulatory effects. Colocalization linked multiple sclerosis risk to AHI1 expression in prenatal neurons and problematic alcohol use to GPX1 expression in postnatal glia. Leveraging dynamic cis-regulatory elements, we identified therapeutic candidates for haploinsufficient neurodevelopmental disorders, including a SOX5 enhancer whose CRISPR activation increased transcript and protein abundance. Together, these findings establish a publicly accessible genomic resource for resolving the developmental and cellular contexts of genetic risk and identifying therapeutic targets in the human brain.

items.title: Sequence-based models predict TF binding with negligible contributions from motif cooperativity
items.abstract: How transcription factors (TFs) selectively recognize their genomic targets among numerous sites containing similar DNA motifs remains an open question. Cooperative binding at neighboring motif sites is widely considered a key mechanism of TF specificity, yet its genome-wide contribution remains unclear. Machine learning models can now predict TF binding directly from DNA sequence, providing opportunities to investigate its underlying determinants. Here, we leveraged BPNet models trained on ~2,000 ENCODE TF binding profiles to systematically assess motif cooperativity. Although detected at individual loci, cooperativity made a negligible contribution to genome-wide binding predictions. Nevertheless, the models captured differences in binding preferences between TFs with similar motif preferences, even within the same cellular environment. These findings highlight the need to critically assess prevailing assumptions and explore alternative mechanisms underlying selective TF binding.

items.title: Pharmacophore-Inspired Virtual Receptor: Generating Realistic Peptide Binding Data for Machine Learning
items.abstract: VReceptor is a virtual receptor simulation framework that generates realistic, sequence-dependent binding data for peptide-based therapeutics. It combines pharmacophore-inspired weighting schemes with amino acid similarity metrics to evaluate peptide design strategies in a controlled environment. Validation using the Prolactin-Releasing Peptide (PrRP) dataset confirms VReceptor's ability to approximate binding behaviours and optimize experimental planning. This framework empowers researchers in computational peptide design and active learning workflows while highlighting areas for further refinement.

items.title: The Xrn1 Rpb4 axis controls mRNA synthesis and imprinting
items.abstract: Co-transcriptional binding (imprinting) of mRNAs by the Rpb4 subunit of RNA polymerase II (RNA pol II) coordinates transcription with cytoplasmic mRNA fates. However, the genomic features of Rpb4-target genes and their cross-talk with decay factors remain unclear. In this study, in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, we demonstrate that genes producing Rpb4-imprinted mRNAs exhibit higher TR paired with lower levels of RNA pol II backtracking. Notably, these loci act as specific genomic targets for the 5'-3' exoribonuclease Xrn1, that has also been shown to act as transcriptional activator in a set of yeast genes, displaying prominent Xrn1 enrichment along their gene bodies. In accordance, XRN1 deletion alters global RNA pol II occupancy, leads to a decrease in TR and reduces growth severely in a rpb4{Delta} background. Furthermore, we show that Rpb4 physically interacts with Xrn1 in a strictly RNA-dependent -imprinting manner. Together, our findings uncover a functional Rpb4 Xrn1 axis that connects efficient transcription elongation with mRNA imprinting and turnover.

items.title: Segment Anything for Microscopy 2
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Computer Science, Georg-August-University Goettingen, Germany
items.abstract: Foundation models have advanced microscopy image segmentation, but existing models are trained on two-dimensional data, struggle with complex structures in volumetric data, and address only a narrow range of analysis tasks. Here we present Segment Anything for Microscopy 2 (SAM2), a foundation model that adapts SAM2 to joint 2D and 3D segmentation in light and electron microscopy. Trained on annotations of more than 23 million cells and nuclei and 1.6 million cellular structures, SAM2 achieves state-of-the-art automatic and interactive segmentation and outperforms generalist and specialist methods on volumetric data. Dedicated models further enable accurate mitochondrion and nucleus segmentation in electron microscopy. Beyond segmentation, SAM2 supports pixel and object classification from few annotations as well as cell tracking in 2D and 3D time-lapse data. All functionality is available in the user-friendly SAM napari plugin. We demonstrated the capabilities of SAM2 on challenging use cases spanning developmental biology, organoid research, cardiac physiology, and histopathology.

items.title: Reduced Resting Brain Entropy and Structural-Functional Reorganization in Hearing Loss
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Psychology, University of Science and Technology of China
items.abstract: Hearing loss changes how the brain processes sound, yet how chronic auditory degradation shapes the temporal organization of spontaneous cortical activity remains unclear. We examined this question using multimodal MRI from 52 adults with age-related hearing loss and 30 normal-hearing controls. Guided by convergent neuroimaging evidence, we focused on the superior temporal gyrus (STG) and assessed brain entropy (BEN), complementary resting-state measures, and gray matter volume (GMV). Hearing loss was associated with lower BEN in a focal right-STG cluster after adjustment for local GMV (14 voxels; cluster FWER p = 0.008), consistent with more recurrent BOLD signal patterns. Six complementary measures of signal amplitude, local synchrony, symbolic sequence diversity, successive variation, and temporal persistence showed no corrected STG differences. A separate whole-brain analysis revealed higher bilateral midcingulate cortex (MCC) GMV (FWE p = 0.002 and 0.015), motivating examination of the auditory-cingulate relationship. The BEN-defined STG region showed stronger focal functional connectivity with MCC (FWE p = 0.031). Exploratory analyses suggested weaker directed STG-to-MCC influence alongside a small tractography-derived group difference. Exploratory directional comparisons indicated stronger right-MCC GMV-BEN coupling (p = 0.034) and STG-MCC SC-FC coupling (p = 0.037) in controls than in hearing loss. Together, these findings link greater temporal regularity in auditory association cortex to altered auditory-cingulate coordination and local structure-function correspondence, suggesting that adaptation to hearing loss involves both the organization of spontaneous cortical dynamics and their relationship to brain structure.

items.title: Rest promotes microglial clearance of degenerating neurons
items.corresponding_institution: The Second Affiliated Hospital of South China University of Technology (Guangzhou First People's Hospital)
items.abstract: How the brain coordinates the removal of degenerating neurons with host rest and activity remains poorly understood. Using longitudinal two-photon imaging in mice with cytosolic TDP-43 proteinopathy, we show that microglia remove neuronal corpses through an ordered sequence of reaching, approaching, isolating and digesting. Clearance was higher during the light (resting) phase and lower during the dark (active) phase. This pattern reversed after light-dark cycle inversion and was blunted by sleep disruption. Chemogenetic inhibition of locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons increased engulfment during the active phase, while activation and inhibition of the {beta}2-adrenergic receptor ADRB2 suppressed and enhanced clearance, respectively, identifying noradrenergic signaling as a brake on engulfment. However, sustained microglial ADRB2 deletion impaired clearance and blunted light-dark differences. These findings reveal that microglial removal of degenerating neurons is enhanced during rest and support a role for noradrenergic signaling in coordinating this cellular maintenance process with the host's rest-activity cycle.

items.title: Altered visual responses in Drosophila BBSome mutants support a nonciliary role in the retina
items.abstract: The BBSome regulates ciliary membrane protein trafficking and mutations in its individual subunits lead in humans, to Bardet-Biedl syndrome, characterized by ciliopathic features including retinal degeneration. Here, we investigated BBSome function in Drosophila melanogaster, whose retinal photoreceptors lack cilia. We used CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis to generate null alleles of six of the conserved BBSome subunits and the associated regulatory molecule BBS3/ARL6. Each single mutant was viable and fertile and only the BBS1-BBS9 double mutant combination showed reduced male fertility. The BBSome mutants retained robust climbing ability and normal ciliary features in their sensory organs. However, all mutant genotypes showed reduced positive phototaxis. Locomotor recordings also demonstrated reduced light responsiveness in the mutants, with a transient suppression of activity during a light pulse in constant darkness. Fluorescently tagged wild-type BBSome subunits formed puncta in differentiating photoreceptors suggesting their association within the developing eye. In the adult mutants, a Rhodopsin 1-GFP reporter showed increased rhabdomeric fluorescence and additional puncta in the photoreceptor cell-body region which were not present in the wild-type. These findings support a non-ciliary contribution of BBSome proteins to orchestrating rhodopsin distribution and determining visual function. The altered localization of rhodopsin 1-GFP is consistent with disrupted rhodopsin trafficking or turnover, through a transport step independent of ciliary axonemes.

items.title: APOE genotype affects the composition of secreted apoE lipoprotein particles and cellular lipid profiles in pericytes
items.abstract: Impairment of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is often observed in Alzheimer's disease patients, especially those who carry the APOE4 allele of apolipoprotein E. Brain pericytes are crucial for maintaining the BBB. Yet, the mechanisms linking APOE genetic variation to pericyte-mediated pathologies are not fully understood. Given the importance of pericyte-secreted factors in cerebrovascular homeostasis, we hypothesized that the protein and lipid compositions of pericyte-secreted apoE lipoproteins (LpEs) would differ depending on the APOE genotype. Using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, we investigated the lipid and protein components of LpEs secreted by human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived APOE-isogenic pericytes. Our results demonstrate that APOE2/E2, APOE3/E3, and APOE4/E4 pericytes secrete LpEs with distinct lipid and protein compositions. ApoE4 particles (LpE4) have high total lipid levels, LpE3 are enriched in ether-linked phospholipids, and LpE2 in ester-linked phosphatidylcholines and short-chain sphingomyelins. Extracellular matrix proteins are highly represented in LpE4, followed by LpE2. In particular, fibronectin is abundant in LpE4 and LpE2, but not in LpE3. While cellular lipid levels and lipid subclass compositions also differ between APOE-isogenic pericytes, they do not mirror the lipid profiles of secreted LpE. The most differentially abundant cellular lipid subclasses include triglycerides, sphingomyelins, glycosphingolipids (Hex3Cer, Hex2Cer, HexCer), and ceramides. In conclusion, the composition of pericyte-secreted LpEs varies by APOE genotype, suggesting distinct functions in brain homeostasis and neurodegenerative disease. Differences in cellular lipids further suggest APOE-mediated changes in lipid metabolism, highlighting the role of vascular cells in brain health and disease.

items.title: Sortilin is a scavenger receptor for cytosolic proteins mislocalized to the extracellular milieu
items.abstract: Aberrant intracellular proteins triggered by various abnormalities, such as misfolding or mislocalization, are degraded by protein quality-control (PQC) systems. However, how extracellular PQC (ePQC) recognizes and eliminates cytosolic proteins -leaked and extracellularly mislocalized upon tissue injury- remains poorly understood. Here, we identify sortilin as a novel ePQC scavenger receptor that preferentially recognizes leaked, non-glycosylated cytosolic proteins in the extracellular space as abnormal and targets them for lysosomal degradation. Through hydrophobic interactions mediated by multiple hydrophobic patches on the sortilin surfaces, sortilin broadly engages diverse cytosolic substrates (e.g., hemoglobin), while discriminating against secreted proteins protected by hydrophilic glycans. Crucially, this clearance is driven by a hit-and-run shuttling mechanism: sortilin resides at the cell surface for only a few minutes, and this rapid cycling, combined with broad-spectrum recognition, enables the degradation of even low-affinity substrates. Together, these findings establish sortilin as an ePQC scavenger receptor for extracellularly mislocalized cytosolic proteins.

items.title: Air and environmental sampling expand metagenomic viral surveillance in Cambodian pig slaughterhouses
items.corresponding_institution: Virology Unit, Institut Pasteur du Cambodge, Pasteur Network, Phnom Penh, Cambodia
items.abstract: Surveillance of viruses in swine depends largely on the sampling of individual animals chosen at random, often limiting detection breadth. Environmental sampling has emerged as an alternative strategy, enabling faster, safer and more cost-effective pathogen monitoring at the human-animal interfaces. Across nine visits to two Cambodian slaughterhouses, we applied metagenomic sequencing to air samples (n = 25), faeces (n = 156), wastewater (n = 15), carcass wash water (n = 18), holding-pen swabs (n = 124), slaughter-box swabs (n = 73) and ropes (n = 16), comparing virus composition to pig snout swabs (n = 193). Combined environmental sampling recovered 96.6% of the viral taxa detected in snout swabs, exceeding 90.9% at every visit. Greater viral diversity was consistently captured in the environment, including swine-associated taxa absent from snout swabs and viral RNA associated with avian and human hosts. Air provided the widest coverage of any single environmental sample type and contributed the largest number of independent virus detections that were not recovered from any other environmental sample. Slaughter-box swabs recovered the fewest taxa, showing that visible contamination with swine material did not correlate with greater viral recovery. Overall, this study identifies air as a pivotal core component of any surveillance program. However, pairing air with additional environmental sample types provides the broadest virus coverage and represents the optimal surveillance strategy in swine slaughterhouses.

items.title: DiGi: An Integer Programming Formulation for Diploid Genome Inference Using a Pangenome Reference
items.abstract: Compared with genotyping against a single linear reference genome, pangenome-based genotyping enables more comprehensive detection of genetic variation, including structural variants. Existing genotyping methods employ a range of combinatorial, probabilistic, and statistical techniques. One class of methods formulates genotyping as a combinatorial path-finding problem in a pangenome graph, allowing bounded recombinations between reference haplotypes. By restricting solutions to mosaics of reference haplotypes, this formulation implicitly exploits linkage disequilibrium. However, extending this formulation to diploid genomes requires jointly identifying two mosaic paths, leading to an exponential increase in the search space. To address this challenge, we first represent the pangenome as a haplotype trellis graph, which maintains reference haplotypes as separate sequences and permits switching between them only at a predefined set of positions. Second, we formulate a combinatorial optimization problem that uses sequencing reads from a target genome to jointly infer a pair of haplotype paths in the graph. We then develop a probabilistic model that automatically sets the optimization parameters based on the read length and coverage of the input data, and an integer programming formulation to solve the resulting problem exactly. Our implementation, DiGi, successfully reconstructs both paternal and maternal copies of 90% of key HLA genes in target genomes absent from the pangenome reference, achieving sequence identity above 99.9%. On the HG002 Genome in a Bottle benchmark, DiGi achieves favorable F1 scores for genotyping SNVs, indels, and structural variants in the highly polymorphic major histocompatibility complex (MHC) region. DiGi remains accurate across a wide range of sequencing coverages, which makes it well suited to population-scale studies with variable coverage across samples.

items.title: FoldMapper: Protein Inverse Folding Model with Structure-Derived Evolutionary Profiles and a Multiscale Graph Encoder
items.abstract: Protein inverse folding designs amino-acid sequences that fold into a target backbone structure. Existing deep-learning methods exploit backbone geometry but not evolutionary statistics. Those statistics come from a multiple sequence alignment, which must be built from a query sequence. That query is the sequence to be designed, so the dependency is circular. We present FoldMapper, an inverse folding model that breaks this circularity. It retrieves structural homologues by shape alone, then aggregates their amino-acid identities into a per-residue structural position-specific frequency (SPSF) profile. A Multiscale Graph Encoder passes a sparse profile-conditioned encoding into a dense structure-conditioned message-passing network. FoldMapper reaches 60.0% best-of-100 sequence recovery on TED domains, 64.9% on PDB, and 51.3%/53.1% on PPIBindBench non-peptide and peptide binders. Across both benchmarks, it lies on the recovery-diversity Pareto front. Structure self-consistency surpasses all baselines on RFdiffusion de novo monomer and binder backbones, and matches the strongest baselines on natural proteins. Ablations and profile-quality analyses show that structure itself encodes recoverable evolutionary information, accessible without a sequence homology search.

items.title: LDEN: Alternating projections for whole genome linkage disequilibrium estimation from next-generation sequencing data
items.abstract: Viral populations often exist as quasispecies of closely-related variants with different mutations. Variants that possess combinations of mutations conferring an overall fitness advantage replicate preferentially. Understanding the true fitness effects of mutations involves disentangling the effects of individual mutations from their genetic background. This problem becomes particularly challenging due to linkage disequilibrium, the non-random association between mutations, which can cause neutral mutations to appear fit and vice versa. Viral populations are typically studied via next-generation sequencing, in which the read length is much shorter than the genome length, rendering long-range linkage disequilibrium unobservable. Estimation of linkage disequilibrium can be performed via population reconstruction, which reconstructs complete sequences before calculating linkage disequilibrium. However, this approach is computationally slow, memory-intensive, and prone to errors, particularly in regions of low coverage. In this work, we present a novel, population reconstruction-independent method for linkage disequilibrium estimation directly from next-generation sequencing data. Our approach uses the observed intra-read linkage disequilibrium values to estimate the unobservable inter-read ones by enforcing mathematical constraints on the linkage disequilibrium matrix. Specifically, because linkage disequilibrium quantifies the covariance between mutant allele frequencies, the linkage disequilibrium matrix must be positive semidefinite. We have formulated linkage disequilibrium estimation as a matrix completion problem and solve it via alternating projections on the constraints of positive semidefiniteness and observed linkage disequilibrium values. This allows the propagation of information from observed intra-read associations to the unobservable inter-read ones without reconstructing the individual variants. We demonstrate that our method yields higher accuracy while being two orders of magnitude faster compared to population reconstruction-based estimation. We demonstrate the performance of the method on both simulated as well as real data showing that it can estimate linkage disequilibrium from a variety of populations.

items.title: A thermoreversible hydrogel model for in situ and ex situ analysis of tumor-immune interactions
items.abstract: Despite the clinical success of cancer immunotherapy, many patients fail to respond or develop resistance, highlighting the need to understand how interactions between tumor and immune cells influence treatment outcomes. Three-dimensional in vitro models allow these interactions to be studied under controlled conditions. However, Matrigel and other biologically derived scaffolds can vary in composition, offer limited independent control over matrix properties, and require cell-recovery procedures that complicate downstream analysis. Here, we present a co-culture model of melanoma spheroids and primary CD8+ T cells based on a defined, thermoreversible synthetic polyisocyanopeptide (PIC) hydrogel. PIC supported T cell viability and migration, with mean motility parameters similar to those in Matrigel and lower variability between experiments. Fluorescence imaging revealed CD8+ T cell infiltration and increased melanoma-cell apoptosis during co-culture. Cooling enabled recovery of nearly all embedded cells in less than 3 min without chemical or enzymatic matrix digestion. Metabolic profiling of recovered T cells identified time-dependent changes in intracellular lactate, amino acids, and tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates, alongside changes in extracellular metabolite availability. Flow cytometry distinguished T cell populations with different effector profiles, with higher expression of effector markers in the fraction associated with melanoma spheroids. By combining a defined synthetic matrix with in situ imaging and rapid recovery for ex situ analysis, this model connects the spatial dynamics of tumor-immune interactions with metabolic and immune phenotypes, providing a basis for studies of immune-cell function and responses to immunotherapy.

items.title: A genetically engineered porcine model of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma captures the biological complexity of the human disease.
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly aggressive cancer with limited treatment options and poor patient outcomes. The lack of clinically relevant large animal models hinders the investigation of early disease mechanisms and translational therapeutic strategies. In this study, we present a genetically engineered porcine PDAC model involving pancreas-specific activation of latent KRASG12D alone (KC) or in combination with TP53R167H (KPC), developed in a midipig background. KC pigs predominantly developed progressive acinar-to-ductal metaplasia (ADM), whereas KPC pigs showed accelerated tumour progression, including PanINs, invasive carcinoma, perineural invasion, and early lymphatic dissemination. Histopathological and molecular analyses revealed pronounced intra- and inter-tumour heterogeneity, a complex stromal microenvironment, and expression of key PDAC markers. Tumours exhibited early alterations in oncogenic KRAS signalling, including increased dosage and differential expression of isoforms, together with dysregulation of tumour suppressor networks involving p16 and TP53 family members. Single-cell transcriptomics and flow cytometric analyses demonstrated an organised and functionally active immune landscape in early lesions, characterised by infiltrating effector and regulatory T-cell populations. Porcine pancreatic cancer cell lines (PoPaCa) were established from KC and KPC tumours, recapitulating key genetic and transcriptional features of the primary lesions. Exploratory drug screening demonstrated heterogeneous responses to clinically relevant and experimental compounds. Responses to gemcitabine and paclitaxel overlapped qualitatively with those observed in human PDAC cell lines, whereas pronounced sensitivity to the GPX4 inhibitor RSL3 and partial responsiveness to trametinib identified testable therapeutic phenotypes for further validation. Together, this genetically engineered porcine PDAC model captures early molecular, cellular, and microenvironmental features of pancreatic tumorigenesis and provides a translational platform to study disease initiation, tumour heterogeneity, immune interactions, and therapeutic response beyond the constraints of rodent models.

items.title: Yin-Yang homeodynamics of Nrf1 and Nrf2: coupling antioxidant defense to redox recovery bistability under persistent stress
items.abstract: This work systematically articulates the Yin-Yang homeodynamics coordination between Nrf1 and Nrf2, resolving the longstanding core paradox in redox biology of why robust Nrf2-mediated antioxidant activation frequently fails to fully eliminate unresolved oxidative stress and re-establish sustained redox homeostasis. Integrating multi-omic expression profiles from human HepG2 cells and primary murine hepatocytes, we constructed an 11-variable endogenous regulatory network model, demonstrating that Nrf2 exclusively mediates transient acute stress attenuation responses, while Nrf1 functions as the non-redundant upstream organiser that supplies the indispensable preconditions for definitive stress resolution via three irreplaceable homeostatic axes: organelle integrity maintenance, proteasome functional recovery, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) cholesterol steady-state handling. Their coupled regulatory interactions generate a bistable configuration demarcated by an index-1 saddle point, partitioning the physiological state space into native low-stress homeostasis and the previously uncharacterised persistent-stress attractor. Once self-amplified unresolved endogenous stress generation reaches dynamic flux balance with Nrf2-dependent clearance at an elevated burden level, the system becomes irreversibly locked in this persistent high-burden equilibrium, and cannot spontaneously return to native homeostatic status even after the initiating upstream disturbance has been fully corrected. Collectively, this study fundamentally delineates the clear functional division between transient antioxidant activation and durable redox recovery during Nrf1/Nrf2 homeodynamics, hence providing a rigorous systems-level theoretical framework to guide future translational interventions targeting redox homeostasis restoration.

items.title: Glutamate/GABA Resource Asymmetry Enables Bidirectional Activity Correction
items.abstract: Glutamate/GABA cotransmission allows one neuron to excite and inhibit the same target. How the two release branches translate a shared spike train into net synaptic drive, and how this drive shapes neural circuit activity, remain unclear. We introduce BRIDGE, a model with separate glutamate and GABA resources that deplete and recover under shared input. The model reproduced glutamatergic depression during repeated stimulation in cotransmission recordings. Late GABAergic responses showed weaker frequency dependence. This asymmetry can generate negative differential gain in the model, allowing faster presynaptic firing to weaken net drive while output remains excitatory. In simulated circuits, cotransmitting neurons shifted their output toward excitation when activity fell and toward inhibition when it rose, improving recovery after perturbations across all circuit sizes tested. Compared with baseline, a simplified spiking implementation yielded higher mean accuracy in most classification comparisons and lower error in selected prediction tasks. Thus, resource asymmetry links firing history to bidirectional correction of circuit activity.

items.title: No allocentric distractor-location learning following self-movement even with contextual anchors and explicit knowledge
items.abstract: Adaptive behavior requires learning where relevant information can likely be found, but also where distraction is likely to occur. For such learning to be useful in everyday life, it must generalize across changing viewpoints as observers move through the environment. Recent work suggests a striking asymmetry in this regard: whereas target-location learning can be grounded in world-centered coordinates, distractor-location learning appears tied to the observer's current viewpoint. One possibility is that allocentric distractor-location learning requires stronger contextual support than allocentric target-location learning. Alternatively, distractor suppression may be fundamentally constrained by viewer-centered spatial coding. To distinguish between these possibilities, participants performed an additional-singleton search task displayed on a tabletop and continuously changed their standing position around the table, while the high-probability distractor location remained fixed in the external environment. Unlike previous studies using this paradigm, contextual anchors were embedded directly within the search display, allowing distractor locations to be encoded relative to a stable task-relevant allocentric structure. In a second experiment, participants were additionally explicitly informed about the distractor-location regularity. Despite task-relevant contextual structure and explicit knowledge, distractor-location learning failed to emerge in world-centered coordinates. Together with previous findings showing robust egocentric distractor-location learning using the same set-up, these findings strengthen the view that learned distractor suppression relies primarily on viewer-centered spatial coding, potentially reflecting a process linked to viewpoint-specific action selection.

items.title: ACC Sulcal Morphology as a Neurodevelopmental Marker of Proactive and Reactive Cognitive Control among Adolescents
items.abstract: Behavioral inhibition (BI) is an early temperament associated with higher risk for later anxiety. BI has been linked to variation in cognitive control, particularly proactive control, a crucial component of executive functions which involves monitoring one's own behavior and adapting that behavior to achieve a particular goal, which may help explain BI's association with elevated anxiety risk. Yet little is known about the neurobiology of cognitive control development among children with BI. Variation in anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) sulcal pattern asymmetry, established prenatally and stable across development, is associated with individual differences in cognitive control. This preliminary study examined whether ACC sulcal symmetry is associated with BI, proactive and reactive control (measured via the AX-CPT) in adolescents. Structural T1-weighted MRI was acquired from 62 adolescents aged 12 to 15 years. ACC patterns in each hemisphere were classified as 'single type' or 'double parallel type' based on the presence of a paracingulate sulcus. Adolescents with symmetric ACC patterns showed lower proactive control (d' context; 2p = .091) and greater reactive control (BX probe interference effect; 2p = .119). These associations held even when tested within the same statistical model and were comparable in magnitude. ACC symmetry was not associated with BI, nor did it interact with BI to predict cognitive control scores. Overall, the findings provide preliminary evidence that ACC sulcal morphology may be a structural marker of variability in cognitive control, with relevance to BI-related neurocognitive risk.

items.title: Intra-thalamic coordination maintains arousability in slow-wave sleep
items.corresponding_institution: Key Laboratory of Brain, Cognition and Education Sciences, Ministry of Education, Institute for Brain Research and Rehabilitation, Guangdong Key Laboratory of M
items.abstract: Slow-wave sleep preserves the capacity for spontaneous or stimulus-evoked awakening despite reduced responsiveness, yet how thalamic nuclei coordinate to preserve arousability remains unclear. We analysed six fMRI and EEG datasets spanning sleep, propofol anesthesia and unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS). During N2 and N3, centromedian (CM) and ventral posterolateral (VPL) nuclei showed convergent edge-community profiles and increased closed-loop intra-thalamic motifs, changes not observed during anesthesia or UWS. During N3, directed effective connectivity along CM[->]VPL[->]pulvinar (PUL) increased versus wakefulness and N2. Stronger CM[->]VPL and VPL[->]PUL connectivity covaried with greater N3 delta power, which was higher before awakening than before transitions to N2 and positively associated with three-month improvement in behavioural responsiveness in UWS. These findings identify a CM-VPL-PUL-centred pattern of intra-thalamic organization linked to preserved arousability during slow-wave sleep, extending accounts focused on individual nuclei and thalamocortical interactions.

items.title: Cross-species phosphoproteomic mapping of mTORC1 signalling reveals RNA splicing regulation during neurodevelopment
items.abstract: Mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) regulates diverse cellular processes through its kinase activity and is essential for nervous system development. Although mTORC1 hyperactivation causes numerous neurodevelopmental disorders, its downstream targets in the developing nervous system remain poorly defined. Here, by profiling thousands of proteins and tens of thousands of phosphosites during the neurogenic phase in mouse and human models, we systematically define the proteomic and phosphoproteomic landscape downstream of mTORC1 during neurodevelopment. To facilitate community access, we developed PhosphoTargets, an interactive platform comprising protein and phosphoprotein expression data from mTORC1 models and patient tissue. We demonstrate the utility of this resource by identifying the deubiquitylating enzyme USP9X as a novel mTORC1 substrate and showing that mTORC1-dependent phosphorylation of USP9X regulates human neural progenitor cell proliferation. Furthermore, integration with gene expression datasets reveals a new role for mTORC1 in the regulation of mRNA splicing. Together, these data provide a comprehensive resource for investigating mTORC1 signalling mechanisms and reveal novel processes through which mTORC1 regulates neurodevelopment.

items.title: Intestinal goblet cell loss induces microbiota-independent mucosal and systemic IgA dysregulation
items.abstract: Goblet cells are essential for establishing the intestinal mucus layer and exert diverse immunomodulatory functions. The mucus barrier cooperates with secretory immunoglobulin A (IgA) to regulate host-microbiota interactions and maintain intestinal immune homeostasis. The extent to which goblet cells directly regulate IgA responses remains unclear. Here, we show that depletion of Muc2-expressing intestinal secretory cells in mice caused barrier dysfunction and intestinal inflammation accompanied by profound mucosal and systemic IgA dysregulation, including hyper-IgA, circulating IgA-IgG immune complexes and renal IgA deposition. Selective Paneth cell depletion did not reproduce these IgA abnormalities, and Muc2-deficient mice showed an intermediate phenotype, implicating loss of goblet-cells rather than Paneth cells or of Muc2 loss in this phenotype. Germ-free rederivation markedly attenuated intestinal inflammation but did not prevent mucosal and systemic hyper-IgA or IgA-IgG immune-complex formation, demonstrating that goblet cell loss drives IgA dysregulation independently of live microbial colonisation. Goblet cell loss and IgA deficiency shaped the mucosa-associated microbiota largely independently, as goblet cell depletion promotes expansion of the genus Akkermansia, whereas IgA deficiency reduced Akkermansia but allowed expansion of Mucispirillum and aggravated colonic pathology, indicating that elevated IgA response is partially protective. These findings reveal goblet cells as critical regulators of mucosal and systemic IgA homeostasis beyond mucus production and point to epithelial-immune interactions as potential contributors to IgA-mediated diseases.

items.title: Spatially-Organized Adaptive Immune Niches in Granulomas Dictate Local Defense and Correlate with Disease Severity in Tuberculosis Patients
items.abstract: The cellular composition and spatial organization of immune responses within tuberculosis (TB) granulomas have been increasingly characterized, yet how these spatially organized immune cell populations coordinate local adaptive immunity remains largely unknown. Here, we integrated single-cell multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics, and immune receptor profiling to construct a comprehensive spatial atlas of human TB granulomas. We identified two concentric adaptive immune niches surrounding the central necrotic core. The outer niche comprised granuloma-associated tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) that supported TFH-B cell interactions and exhibited functional germinal center-like features associated with antigen-driven B-cell maturation toward FCRL5 antibody-producing cells. The inner niche contained antigen-experienced and Mtb-reactive effector memory CD8 T cells (TEM), which were recruited from distal lung regions by LGALS9high chemokine-expressing macrophages and activated to undergo local clonal expansion. In lgals9l1 deficient zebrafish, macrophage depletion was accompanied by marked reductions in T- and B-cell enrichment within granulomas and increased bacterial loads, supporting a role for LGALS9high macrophages in coordinating local adaptive immunity against TB infection. Finally, AI-based prediction of spatial gene expression from clinical hematoxylin and eosin-stained specimens revealed that inferred TLS abundance increased with TB disease severity. These findings identify spatially interconnected adaptive immune niches that organize protective immune responses within human TB granulomas, therefore providing a foundation for understanding granuloma adaptive immunity and developing host-directed therapies and vaccines for TB (https://tbomics.smart-nbc.org.cn/).

items.title: The decidual microenvironment shapes neutrophil subsets that promote extravillous trophoblast invasion in early pregnancy
items.abstract: Successful establishment of the maternal-fetal interface is a critical process during early pregnancy, ensuring healthy fetal development. A critical phase in establishing the utero-placental blood supply is the invasion of extravillous trophoblasts (EVTs) into the maternal spiral arteries, marking the transformation of the endometrium into the decidua. By separating the EVT invaded decidua (iDec) and EVT non-invaded decidua (niDec), we demonstrate that neutrophils dominate the iDec immune landscape during early human pregnancy. High-dimensional flow cytometry and single-cell transcriptomics revealed that the decidualized microenvironment extends neutrophil survival and shapes discrete tissue-resident subsets, including an activated CD63high phenotype. Imaging mass cytometry uncovered a precise spatial organization, demonstrating preferential cell-cell interactions between these activated neutrophils and invading EVTs. Furthermore, functional in vitro assays demonstrated that the neutrophil secretome, including the core granular protease neutrophil elastase, directly stimulates EVT invasion. Together, these findings identify decidua-associated neutrophils as crucial cellular coordinators of human placental development.

items.title: NRF2 regulates a lipofuscin-like granule cycle through autophagy-dependent clearance in retinal pigment epithelium
items.corresponding_institution: iNOVA4Health, NOVA Medical School|Faculdade de Ciências Médicas, NMS|FCM, Universidade Nova de Lisboa, Lisboa, Portugal
items.abstract: Lysosomal dysfunction in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells is one pathological aspect of retinal degenerative disorders, which contribute to the buildup of autofluorescent undegraded materials such as lipofuscin. A comprehensive understanding of lipofuscin biology remains a critical gap in the field. Here, we explore the cell biology of lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granules (AFGs) within RPE cells and the potential of nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) activation to promote its clearance in human RPE cells. Under steady-state conditions we find that photoreceptor outer segments (POS) phagocytosis by the RPE is sufficient to trigger NRF2 activation, suggesting a feedback mechanism that links phagocytic activity with cytoprotective stress responses. RPE fed with excess POS accumulate lipofuscin-like autofluorescent granules (AFG) within hours, a measure of lysosomal dysfunction. These AFGs gradually loose connection with the endocytic system and remain as ''storage granules'' within RPE. Pre-treatment or delayed pharmacological activation of NRF2 with dimethyl fumarate (DMF) significantly decrease accumulation of AFGs, suggesting improved clearance mechanisms. Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of autophagy totally abolish these effects. Similarly, compromised autophagy also abolished the clearance effects observed with inhibition of the mTOR pathway. Collectively, these results suggest a 3-step lipofuscin cycle within the RPE (formation, storage and clearance), provide mechanistic evidence that autophagy is an essential process for the clearance of AFGs and that NRF2-activation and other stimulators of autophagy may represent novel therapeutic strategies to restore RPE homeostasis and mitigate retinal degeneration.

items.title: MTCH2 drives metabolic remodeling in muscle satellite cells via mitochondrial fatty acid utilization
items.corresponding_institution: School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, University of Shizuoka
items.abstract: Muscle satellite cell (MuSC) differentiation into myoblasts underpins skeletal muscle regeneration by supporting myofiber repair and formation. This process involves extensive metabolic remodeling from glycolysis to mitochondrial oxidative metabolism. Although this switch is required for proper MuSC differentiation, its molecular regulators remain unclear. Here, we identify mitochondrial carrier homolog 2 (MTCH2) as a regulator of this remodeling. MTCH2 contributes preferentially to MuSC differentiation rather than proliferation and supports mitochondrial respiration, particularly under a low-glucose condition. Loss of Mtch2 fragments mitochondria and suppresses respiration associated with fatty acid {beta}-oxidation. Notably, MTCH2-dependent fatty acid utilization appears largely independent of carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT1). Furthermore, skeletal muscle regeneration is impaired in MuSC-specific Mtch2 conditional knockout mice. Together, these findings establish MTCH2 as a regulator of mitochondrial metabolic remodeling in MuSCs and highlight its context-dependent roles in cellular metabolism and function.

items.title: Selenite transport by SLC26A6 contributes to redox homeostasis and ferroptosis resistance
items.corresponding_institution: Rudolf Virchow Center for Integrative and Translational Bioimaging, University of Wuerzburg, Wuerzburg, Germany
items.abstract: Selenium is an essential micronutrient widely found in dietary supplements and fortified foods and is required for selenoprotein synthesis and function. Although the molecular mechanisms of selenium-dependent selenoprotein translation are well understood, its uptake mechanisms remain only partially characterized. Using a CRISPR-based loss-of-function screen, we identify the solute carrier SLC26A6 as a direct selenite transporter. Using biochemical, cellular, and in vivo studies, we show that SLC26A6 directly transports selenite and promotes selenoprotein translation, redox homeostasis, and ferroptosis resistance. Additionally, we report the first human-specific SLC26A6 inhibitor and determine the structure of the SLC26A6-inhibitor complex by cryo-electron microscopy. These findings identify a previously uncharacterized route of inorganic selenium uptake and establish SLC26A6 as a pharmacologically tractable determinant of selenoprotein synthesis, redox homeostasis, and ferroptosis resistance.

items.title: Comparative chemogenetic profiling of Hedgehog pathway inhibitors reveals class-specific genetic modifiers
items.abstract: Chemogenetic profiling is a powerful method to dissect compound-gene interactions and to reveal a compound's mechanism of action and possible resistance mechanisms. Here, we extended the use of chemogenetic profiling beyond cytotoxic compounds to classify non-toxic inhibitors of the Hedgehog signaling pathway. We performed Hedgehog pathway-focused genetic screens in NIH/3T3 mouse fibroblasts using two chemically distinct inhibitors each of Smoothened (SMO) and BET bromodomain proteins. The resulting chemogenetic profiles revealed class-specific modifiers, with loss of Mosmo conferring resistance to SMO inhibitors, and loss of Paxip1 conferring resistance to BET bromodomain inhibitors. Beyond these compound-specific effects, we show how loss of Nf2, Paxip1, or Mosmo differentially impacts Hedgehog pathway transduction upstream, at the level of the cilium, and/or downstream, at the level of transcription. Together, the Mosmo- and Paxip1-knockout lines provide new tools for epistasis mapping, and the profiling strategy a route to mechanism-of-action studies for inhibitors of ciliary signaling.

items.title: p53 supports healthy aging
items.corresponding_institution: Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program; Sanford Burnham Prebys MDI; La Jolla, CA, USA
items.abstract: p53 is a master regulator of cellular stress responses that is also implicated in the aging process. Its role in aging is often considered an example of antagonistic pleiotropy (AP), where it acts beneficially as a tumor suppressor early in life, but detrimentally in late life, for example by driving accumulation of stress-associated, pro-inflammatory senescent cells. However, the causal role of p53 in aging is not well-defined, and the AP model has not been definitively tested through loss- of-function studies. Here we show, contrary to the prediction of AP, that p53 promotes healthy aging in mouse liver by suppressing excessive inflammation and maintaining metabolic function. Multimodal RNA, protein, epigenetic and spatial profiling at the single-cell level in aged mouse liver confirmed age-dependent increase in p53 pathway activation. Hepatocyte-specific knockout of p53 in livers of aged mice, but not of young mice, increased inflammation and immune infiltration. Mechanistically, p53 suppressed DNA replication stress and DNA damage, known precursors to inflammatory signaling. In aged hepatocytes, p53 also directly targeted and maintained expression of metabolic genes, and knockout of p53 sensitized aged mice to metabolic stress-induced liver damage. Complementing these loss-of-function data, pharmacological activation of p53 with the small-molecule MDM2 inhibitor HDM201 in aged mice reversed age-associated suppression of metabolic genes, decreased age-associated inflammation and delayed onset of frailty. These results identify p53 activity in aged tissue as protective rather than degenerative. Importantly, this protective function is pharmacologically targetable, potentially for the benefit of healthy aging in humans.

items.title: Disruption to rRNA biogenesis triggers histone mRNA 3' misprocessing in C. elegans through genome-surveillance regulators
items.abstract: Maturation of replication-dependent histone pre-mRNA transcripts involves a 3' cleavage event facilitated by the conserved stem-loop binding protein (SLBP). Cellular conditions that trigger an error in this process are not well understood. Here, we developed a GFP-based in vivo histone 3' misprocessing reporter in Caenorhabditis elegans and performed a genome-wide RNAi screen for histone regulators. We found that depletion of genes involved in various steps of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) biosynthesis triggers misprocessing of histone 3' tail, with the strongest effect observed upon depletion of rpoa-2 encoding the core subunit of RNA polymerase I. Transcriptome sequencing reveals rpoa-2 knockdown mirrors the effect of depleting the C. elegans SLBP homologue CDL-1 at the protein level, indicating that rpoa-2 and CDL-1 co-regulate similar transcriptome targets. Depletion of rpoa-2 impairs endomitosis of the C. elegans intestinal cells and is accompanied by aberrant activation of cell cycle markers in the absence of change in DNA content. Gene interaction analysis shows that rpoa-2 signals through multiple conserved cell cycle regulators, including ATM-1, GEN-1, and LIN-35 to trigger histone misprocessing in both CDL-1 dependent and independent manners. Together, our findings reveal that disruption in the rRNA biogenesis pathway triggers histone misprocessing through conserved genome surveillance pathway regulators.

items.title: RNA polymerase II links arsenic exposure to chromosome-wide γH2A signaling
items.abstract: Arsenic is a widespread environmental carcinogen whose genotoxicity is commonly attributed to oxidative DNA damage and replication-associated lesions. Here, we identify RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) as an important determinant of early arsenic-induced DNA damage checkpoint signaling. In budding yeast, acute As(III) exposure induced rapid, chromosomewide {gamma}H2A accumulation under low oxidative stress, without requiring ongoing bulk DNA replication or causing detectable chromosome fragmentation. Unexpectedly, depletion of Rpb1, the largest subunit of RNAPII and a key component of its catalytic center, markedly attenuated this response. Comparison of different transcriptional perturbations revealed that only selected disruptions of RNAPII function, including Rpb1 inactivation in the rpb1-1 mutant, induced widespread {gamma}H2A accumulation. These contrasting effects suggest that checkpoint activation depends on the presence and particular functional states of RNAPII. Consistent with its involvement, As(III) reduced RNAPII chromatin occupancy and Rpb1 abundance, while arsenic-affinity assays recovered the RNAPII complex. However, As(III) did not measurably inhibit RNA elongation by purified RNAPII in vitro. In human cells, acute As(III) exposure induced ATR phosphorylation and {gamma}H2AX accumulation under low-ROS conditions, while pharmacological inhibition of transcription also triggered {gamma}H2AX phosphorylation. Together, our findings establish an important contribution of RNAPII to early arsenic-induced checkpoint signaling and suggest that the transcription machinery can couple environmental stress to a chromosome-wide DNA damage response.

items.title: Pharmacological and genetic access to astrocytic cholesterol programs in human neural cells
items.abstract: Astrocyte-neuron interactions coordinate cholesterol metabolism, cell adhesion, and synaptic gene expression1,2, and related gene expression programs decline together in schizophrenia3. Whether pharmacological or genetic perturbations can selectively engage components of this coordinated biology was unknown. Here we combine genetically diverse cultures of human stem-cell-derived neurons and astrocytes, pharmacological profiling, genetic association mapping and CRISPR interference to examine these biological programs. In stem-cell-derived astrocyte mono-cultures, the antipsychotic clozapine induced a focused transcriptional response involving cholesterol biosynthesis and export, and drove an increase in intracellular and secreted cholesterol. This response overlapped with the cholesterol-related component of the astrocytic response to neuronal contact seen in neuron-astrocyte co-cultures, but did not extend to synaptic cell-adhesion genes. In neuron-astrocyte co-cultures, clozapine also increased neuronal firing. Across individual cell donors, cholesterol-pathway induction by clozapine was broadly shared but varied in magnitude. Gene-expression patterns in untreated donors were associated with differential responses to clozapine and the liver X receptor agonist GW3965. Common genetic variation influenced expression of several cholesterol-related genes, including a clozapine-dependent association of HSD17B7 expression with nearby genetic variants. Independently, repression of LDLR induced coordinated expression of cholesterol-biosynthesis genes in astrocytes that overlapped with astrocyte responses to clozapine and neuronal contact. These findings identify shared cholesterol-related transcriptional responses to pharmacological and genetic perturbations and link common genetic variation to distinct features of cholesterol-pathway responses.

items.title: Genetic regulation of ALK inhibitor response in diverse human cell types
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Medicine, University of Chicago, Chicago, IL, USA
items.abstract: Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) inhibitors are effective treatments for ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer but cause diverse adverse events affecting multiple tissues. Genetic variation may contribute to inter-individual differences in susceptibility, but the small number of treated patients limits the power of genetic association studies. Moreover, the diversity of affected tissues and cell types makes functional investigation challenging. We used induced pluripotent stem cells from 49 individuals to generate heterogeneous differentiating cultures (HDCs) containing multiple cell types, treated them with five ALK inhibitors (crizotinib, alectinib, ceritinib, brigatinib, and lorlatinib) for 24 hours, and characterized transcriptional responses using single-cell RNA sequencing. These responses showed cell-type-specific and shared transcriptional effects. Integrating gene expression with individual genotypes, we identified 4,371 expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) across 21 cell types, including 2,137 response eQTLs whose regulatory effects differ between untreated and drug-treated cells. These results nominate candidates for future studies of ALK inhibitor toxicity.

items.title: S-PLM-TM enables fast and accurate sequence-based search for remote homologs
items.abstract: Protein structures and functions can remain conserved after extensive sequence divergence, but detecting these distant relationships across large databases remains challenging. Here we present S-PLM-TM, a sequence-only remote homology search tool based on a structure-aware protein language model. Cross-modal flow matching and contrastive learning incorporate structural information into sequence representations. A lightweight calibration head enables structural-similarity search with the frozen encoder, while a residue-level alignment head generates structural alignments directly from sequence. S-PLM-TM outperforms the tested sequence-based methods in remote homology detection, rivals structure-based methods in structural classification and retrieves the most functionally consistent neighbors. It also retrieves distantly related enzymes with shared catalytic functions at a level comparable to the best-performing structure-based methods. In large-scale database search, S-PLM-TM achieves the highest average precision among both sequence-based and alignment-free methods, with speed approaching the fastest sequence-alignment tools. Together, these results establish S-PLM-TM as a practical tool that combines sensitive and biologically informative remote homology search with the speed required for database-scale retrieval.

items.title: Quantum Machine Learning for Missense Variant Pathogenicity Prediction in the KCNQ Gene Family
items.abstract: Missense variants in the KCNQ family of voltage-gated potassium channel genes are associated with a broad spectrum of neurological and cardiac disorders for which computational tools capable of differentiating benign and pathogenic variants are essential. Here, we present, to our knowledge, the first application of quantum machine learning (QML) to missense pathogenicity prediction. We employ a hybrid quantum framework combining data re-uploading quantum neural networks with quantum support vector machines and applied it to pathogenicity classification across the full KCNQ gene family. Systematic exploration of circuit architectures revealed that optimal hyperparameter choices enable the proposed quantum model to achieve predictive performance superior to or comparable to state-of-the-art classical machine learning approaches, reaching AUC-ROC values of approximately 0.94 across the full dataset. Although no clear quantum advantage is observed at present, these results demonstrate that quantum feature representations can effectively capture biologically relevant patterns in variant data and establish QML as a viable framework for future applications in computational genomics and precision medicine.

items.title: QT-RelCor: Statistical Inference for Comorbidity of Quantitative Traits and Disease from Related Individuals
items.abstract: Background: Complex diseases with a high genetic component often cluster in families and are associated with quantitative traits (QT-s) such as endophenotypes showing comorbidity with the end-point disease trait. Detecting associations with such QT-s can provide a non-invasive approach to indicate disease onset at an early stage, or help in tracking disease severity. Traditional case-control studies generally involve unrelated individuals, which can introduce heterogeneity due to varying lifestyle and exposure patterns. Often QT values may be available from related individuals such as families of affected probands. In these situations, assessment of comorbidity restricting to unrelated cases and controls leads to unnecessary loss of power. On the other hand, ignoring the correlation structure of families leads to grossly incorrect confidence intervals impacting both type 1 error and power of tests. Yet, these practices are common in the absence of standard inference procedures for such data. Methods: We propose statistical procedures for analyzing clustered data to infer association between the QT-s and the binary trait. The methods allow a mix of families and unrelated cases and utilizes all available individuals. In particular, two novel competing approaches are proposed and evaluated: a parametric approach based on multivariate normal likelihood and a non-parametric approach that combines the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with a modified version of the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results: We conducted simulation studies to assess type 1 error and power across multiple scenarios, which demonstrated the robustness of the proposed tests. Both the tests perform considerably better than both the classical t-test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test under both parametric and non-parametric settings. We illustrate the proposed methods by applying them on sibship data from the Centre for Brain and Mind program to identify a number of quantitative precursors significantly associated with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Conclusion: In summary, the proposed methods provide a robust and powerful approach to detect comorbid endophenotypes incorporating data from families of affected individuals. Findings from the analysis of sibling-based data on schizophrenia and bipolar disorder support role of a few selected neurocognitive assessments as potential markers of these disorders.

items.title: Automated segmentation of renal structures using brightfield images of unstained kidney biopsies
items.corresponding_institution: INESC TEC, Faculty of Engineering, University of Porto, Porto, Portuga
items.abstract: The automated segmentation of unstained kidney brightfield microscopy images remains a significant challenge in medical imaging. In conventional histopathology, staining provides crucial structural and molecular contrast, allowing renal compartments and structures to be readily distinguished. The absence of staining markedly reduces this contrast, obscuring the fine architectural details that are essential for diagnosis. Addressing this gap would reduce reliance on staining protocols, reduce technical and interpretive variability, and preserve valuable tissue for downstream molecular or multi-omics analyses. Ultimately, automation of unstained image segmentation could enable faster, more objective tissue analysis while preserving samples for further molecular testing. In this work, we provide a comprehensive review of state-of-the-art segmentation methods applied to renal brightfield microscopy images. Current findings highlight a predominance of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) based architectures for semantic segmentation approaches while recent trends point to the growing application of transformer-based and instance-segmentation strategies. However, the field is still hampered by the scarcity and poor annotation of publicly available renal datasets. Aiming to further contribute to the enhancement of the field, a dataset of 18 Whole Slide Images (WSIs) of unstained human kidney tissue is made publicly available. Additionally, in the dataset, we provide 543 annotated tiles extracted from the WSIs, facilitating further research into stain-independent segmentation approaches. As a third contribution, we present a preliminary case study, evaluating state-of-the-art deep learning segmentation architectures, including U-Net and Segment Anything Model (SAM). Our preliminary results indicate that deep learning models demonstrate promising segmentation performance in unstained kidney biopsies. In alignment with these findings, advanced customised loss functions and data augmentation were integrated into the supervised training of the promising U-Net, DeepLabv3+, and TransUNet models, achieving significant improvements compared to the baseline experiments. To exploit the abundance of unlabelled data, we further tested FixMatchSeg, a semi-supervised learning method; however, its segmentation performance remained slightly behind the supervised methods. Taken together, these contributions establish a foundation for future research in stain-independent Computational Pathology, demonstrating that unstained brightfield microscopy images can reliably support downstream tissue analysis tasks. Our dataset, validation experiments, and methodological insights provide the community with both resources and benchmarks to advance robust, data-efficient, and generalisable kidney tissue segmentation.

items.title: Deciphering the Biological Function of Tandem Mass Spectra Using a Dual-Modal Metabolite Language Model
items.abstract: Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry untargeted metabolomics captures thousands of metabolic peaks from biological samples. Conventional identification-dependent metabolomics workflows require confident structural annotation before identified features can enter downstream pathway or functional analysis. However, only a small fraction of detected metabolic features can be assigned confident structural annotations, leaving a large fraction difficult to incorporate into downstream biological interpretation, a form of "functional dark matter". Here, we introduce Spec2Function, a function-centric framework that infers biological functions from tandem mass spectrometry (MS2) spectra. Spec2Function is trained using characterized spectrum-text pairs but does not require prior structural identification of the query spectra at inference time. At its core is Spec2Biotext, a dual-encoder contrastive model that embeds MS2 spectra and curated multi-aspect natural language functional texts into a unified functional space. Combined with a retrieval-augmented generation framework grounded in curated databases and biomedical literature, Spec2Function retrieves evidence-grounded biological knowledge and produces coherent functional summaries for individual spectra or groups of spectra. Across metabolite- and pathway-level benchmarks, Spec2Function achieved higher similarity to reference functional descriptions than the evaluated comparators and expanded the fraction of the metabolome accessible to functional interpretation. Application to a human liver cirrhosis cohort recapitulated known metabolic alterations and identified additional literature-supported functional modules.
